Councillor Misra & Co,

My family, the Williams and later Buckler family, lived at Great House Farm
(Tŷ Mawr) beside St Dochdwy's for almost 4 consecutive centuries until
1988, when our 800 year old 10 bed manorial home was subject to an SAS
style siege and demolished. I was born there. The site is now Church View
Close.

That whole incident appears to stem from a 1955 possession order for a
parcel of land east of the parcel we held freehold of. The order contained
ambiguity that was later misinterprited to make our occupancy of our parcel
appear permissive, following our paper title copy being stolen. A 1962
possession order for our parcel was created based on that but not enforced
on my disabled, widow grandmother. Who just had a leg amputated in 1955.
Instead the interest in the 1962 order was conveyed from Western Ground
Rents to BP in 1969. BP altered the ordinance survey, shifting the
descriptor from their parcel onto my nans. And appending "farm' to it. They
again made her occupancy appear pernissive in 1974 with their famous
licence letters. Then conveyed interest in that, again, to their own sister
company in 1975. Not withstanding the possession of the 1962 order was
quashed in 1974. Also in 1974 my nans ownership claim was not legally
exstiguished and instead the court ajourned. In 1983 BP then quietly
registered our land in their names at the land registry, failing to
disclose my nans ownership claim, she also died in the 2 weeks she will
have had to challenge them. She had not been known to not challenge them in
decades of her campaigning. Land registry also didn't notify her/ us. BP
then merged our parcel into theirs, as my nan fought for her life and died.
The land registry wrote to the MP this week claiming not find anything
wrong with the role they played in 1982/1983. .

In 1877 title became our families from Daniel Thomas & Son. But not until
1928 when quarrying completed on the land. In 1916 Bute produced an
agrictural tenancy for our family featuring our occupied parcel and a
parcel to the east. The interest in this is what conveyed to Western Ground
Rents in 1938. And in 1939 they revised the agreement for the parcel east
of ours. And excluded ours parcel from any tenancy due to the 1928 event
and my great grandads registration of the freehold.

The 1877 - 1928 agreement and title deed was stolen from our home according
to my late nans statement in these proceedings.

When WGR saught possession of their parcel to the east of ours in 1955,
they exercised moral hazard to introduce ambiguity into the order,
considering my nans vulnerable state (amputee, widow, pensioner, stolen
title deed), which could have and did get later misinterprited to make my
nans occupancy appear permissive. And Western Ground Rents the owner. Thus
fabricating a defective title with the 1962 possession order for my nans
parcel and through conveying that unenforced possession order to BP in
1969. BPs permissive occupancy licence in 1974 and 1975 conveyance repeated
that process to make interest transfer and a title chain emerge, with no
root title.

Mr Paul Egan answered a request from me on 14 June this year. He searched
the Council's records, explained that the minute books from 1982 onward
were deposited with Glamorgan Archives in 2002, set out the section 21
position correctly, and pointed me to the Council's own pages on buildings
of significance in the community. He also told me something I had not known
— that before 1982 Llandough came under Penarth Town Council — which has
opened a line of research I would otherwise have missed. I had written to
him in strong terms and he replied with courtesy and care anyway. I
understand he has since retired after long service to the village. Please
pass on my thanks if you are able to. I am not asking the Council to
revisit his answer; it was a proper one.

I am assembling a complete documentary and photographic record of my
family's old manorial 10-bedroom birth and family home since 1667, at the
centre of that church you British built in the 1800s — I am interested in
everything: planning, archaeology, land registration, family papers, oral
memory — all into a single, centralised searchable archive. So the actual
full story can be retold. Warts and all.

Please bear with me for the rest of my email. I was traumatised by our
experience being dispossessed in the 80's. We've seen no justice. My family
died challenging any of the false narrative. And the remaining alive won't
speak up. The State have tried covering this up and continue to do so for
decades too. I'm the first to try to bring this all to light.

My intent with all this is a Welsh heritage project I have underway in
Patagonia, Argentina, where a replica of my old farm is to be constructed
as a museum.

In Argentina they are different from you British currently occupying us
Welsh in Wales, in that they celebrate and don't supress or conceal our
Welsh heritage, culture, language, history. It is very refreshing for me
there, as an indigenous Briton who was brutally torn from my ancestral
birthland in 1988, in what can only be described as ethnic cleansing. I am
not even exaggerating; the particulars of the horrors done to my family
there make reconstructing the full chronology very challenging. It's not
new what Brit'ish do to indigenous people globally, or the Welsh
historically. But we were maybe the last to be annexed, colonised and
looted in such a systematic and brutal way.

It would be passable if we were sincerely squatters being evicted as the
press reported. Or even courts believed. But the land BP possessed they
had. We lost the parcel east of ours fair and square. They came to occupy
our neighbouring land and home too out of greed, to build Church View
Close. Using force, stealth/ secrecy and license. The destinction would
have been clear had BP not registered our land in their names and merged
ours into theirs, in such a clandestine way, in 1982/1983.

So much of my family's and people's history and heritage in Llandough
continues to be completely covered up in lieu of those 20 characterless
(Church View Close) concentration work-camp houses, without so much as a
park-bench plaque to commemorate any of the following:

- the 1,026 medieval burials
- Marconi staying with us while inventing radio
- Peerless Joe Driscoll fighting his first fight in our barn
- the Roman villa
- Christian monastery
- 2,200-year-old Celtic roundhouse

the list goes on. The LiDAR scans etc.

I find it abhorrent that the Llandough website history page does not
mention any of this either. I know the British are proud of their No.1
invention: the concentration work camp — but it is sad witnessing all our
towns and cities being turned into them. Not that I am on the British Isles
much, except occasionally as a sort of autochthonous Django Unchained.
Seeing all the voters being imported to keep the kinds of governors,
Princess of Darkness and demons the Bible warns us about in power does not
even sadden me anymore. I think crusades may happen sooner as a result, and
therein resides my hope for my small pale island.

It was not always such a demonic realm for us natives, nor our
non-indigenous actual guests, friends and family in Llandough. My family
lived in the main manorial house in Llandough consecutively since 1667
until the British's highly illegal, unlawful and unconstitutional siege and
theft of our stronghold in 1988. We still appear to own the land under
Church View Close. You British only awarded yourselves possession of our
Christian stronghold. Possession being the weapon of choice of a demonic
realm. When I was a soldier in Cyprus I would enjoy watching the UN hand
back stolen, occupied land to the Greeks and Turks. I look forward to that
occurring when Wales literally, not figuratively, decolonises. Or Scotland
renounces. Or Ireland unites. I see the British State as more of a
terrorist organisation than the IRA, and I think it is the British State we
need to stop harbouring on our motherland.

In the interim of revolution, I hold some faith in coalitions. Namely
thanks to Councillor Chris Franks, my grandmother's old good friend of
decades, who at least acknowledged my email. And that a grave injustice
does appear to have occurred to my family and, as a matter of public
interest, others too. To be brutally honest I think my case shows signs we
are in a landmark bubble and a land-market crash is coming. This racket of
converting amputee, disabled widow pensioners' occupancy of our lands from
freehold to permissive (with ambiguity and misinterpretation and fraud and
concealment) possession orders and conveyance, stealth/secrecy etc. — was
not a sustainable viable way of annexing. You can fool some of the people
some of the time. But not all of the people all of the time.

But this is a request for co-operation with reconstructing history, not a
complaint. And history which has already been driven to lands many
thousands of miles away, so it can remain buried in the British's wardrobe
of skeletons as you so wish.

With 99% of British MPs refusing to sign EDM 2025 condemning decapitating
Christians, I think Argentina is an apt location for my replica manorial
house, notwithstanding Michael Jones who founded the settlement in
Patagonia had followers who even nicknamed the reason for it as being the
"decapitation committee" here on the British Isles (a century after we
acquired my birth home in Llandough, so some time in the late 1700s).

In the interests of being straight with you: I had difficulty getting
replies from the Vale ward member, Councillor George Carroll, and earlier
this year I made a formal complaint to the Vale of Glamorgan about that.
Which I was surprised at after he got thrown out of a council meeting for
being against the City of Sanctuary scheme. My motto is, if you are not on
a government watchlist by now, you should be ashamed of yourself.

I am already resigned to flying in and out of this small formerly pale
island, like it is another military tour of the Middle East. I actually do
not harbour much ill will; I am just sad it has gone to the dogs and half
expect a nuclear strike, flood or crusade.

My advice to my followers is not even to keep defending the concentration
work camps our hijacked towns and cities have been turned into. Instead I
encourage soldiers under my command to enjoy exile or mass exodus. There is
plenty in the British organisations' cells/camps and networks' own rules
which permits corps and exodusers. That way everyone's happy.

The British State is not the first regime to go rogue. Terrorist
organisations (now the official government) like in Afghanistan also have
hostages and prisoners of war who are masochist submissives, like
British/UK citizens. And it is a situationship that suits both parties. But
not something I would want to get in the middle of or encourage others to
get in the middle of. I do not know why so many do.

I am persuaded to organise veterans to attend funerals of casualties of the
civil war our infiltrated, hijacked and traitor-filled regimes waged on
indigenous Britons, with its biological weapons, hybrid warfare, ethnic
cleansing and so forth. And we simply wear our uniforms and salute the
casualties. It is some remedy for the grieving families who, even if
speaking out from the decades of being terrorised into silence, face
decades of being stonewalled from justice from the State. So I am all about
the peaceful, legal and lawful paths forward — as a bona fide, certified,
experienced military commander, leader and warfare professional.

I have seen Councillor Carroll's recent social media posts standing in
front of the photograph of my old farm's only public photo that hangs in
the Merry Harrier pub. If it is in good faith and support I am glad.
Anything less I would not be surprised. Only disappointed. But I extend the
benefit of the doubt with my farm case, because it is a complex case. Even
in my profession as a seasoned cyber/electronic military warfare
professional I find it colossal to navigate.

What I would be grateful for from you who occupy and rule my land, in place
of your Pharisee predecessors, is a coalition with counter-officers such as
myself.

Does your occupying forces/council hold any records that were created after
2002 and therefore not part of the 2002 deposit, concerning our stolen,
occupied Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr/Cedfin)/Church View Close land?

And I should add: suspected, as I am still gathering evidence and
investigating. Albeit it all looks damning for the British and many native
traitors already, and I am only scratching the surface of what happened in
Llandough. My ancestral birthland would not be the first to be looted by
the British and I am doubtful it will be the last. Our SAS-looted treasures
are actually now all captive in British museums. And our SAS-looted
furniture, all from Cardiff Castle, are also held hostage or in circulation
too.

My focus and what I require of your Council, as but a humble (registered to
vote) constituent of the home we got in Dinas Powys and have lived in since
our land became illegally occupied by the British in 1988 — is the village
green in front of St Dochdwy's — including registered village green VG 41,
which your Council raised formally with the Vale when the Great House Farm
site came forward for planning in 1989.

By constituent I do mean I am happy to play the role of a member of society
in a democracy. Albeit it is largely now pageantry and being made a mockery
of in my estimation. I see something very different going on here, i.e. a
terrorist/hostage situationship. And I do not play the role of a hostage or
prisoner of war well — at all! Nor am I a masochist submissive and much
like kissing ring fingers or bending knees. My 22 in Oath ended in 2024
(employed under the Vale of Glamorgan Council too, by some freak
coincidence). So I will thank you in advance not to ask weird stuff of me.
I am nice until it is time not to be. And I believe we are all equal under
law and God.

My family have endured enough force, stealth/secrecy and licence from the
British in the 80s to last us a lifetime. And having been behind a machine
gun in a helicopter in the Middle East, and trained on explosives and
weapons and cyber/electronic warfare capabilities for my military career,
which I left with full honours, I am well aware of how the British regime
operates and human-farms and projects its force. I once had Britain's very
own woke mind virus walking through my mind with its muddy boots. I hope
you all get better too.

Better your cell/network/camp just skip to bringing guns and trying to
force me at gunpoint if you demand anything of me that contrasts
co-operation or coalition. I have seen already a lot of local authorities,
even South Wales Police, opting for clandestine and shadowy silence and
violence, rather than just responding to public FOIs. I think your regime's
attempt to keep our Llandough farm story from ever seeing the light of day
is understandable. But I do find people from time to time, even Iraqis in
Iraq, even myself as a former British soldier, wanting to choose the right
side of history rather than allegiance to a sinking rat ship.

Any record of works carried out on the green and the roadside verge by the
churchyard wall in the mid-1980s is all I am asking for. I hold colour
photographs of trees being removed, spoil carted away and new kerbstones
laid; vehicle registrations in them date the works to between about 1983
and 1990, on more than one occasion. (See attached.) Councillor Carroll's
months of non-response to this specific request to find this information
out was not going to stop me finding all this out. Asking for transparency
and co-operation is mainly a courtesy and formality, seeing as I am a
seasoned military cyber/electronic warfare professional. Going on 30 years
now in fact.

My great-grandfather planted a tree on that green to mark my family's claim
to that land, and my family believe that tree was lost in the work of
making that green, i.e. possible further destruction of evidence, possibly
nothing. I should be clear that the green does not even appear to fall
inside the boundary of land we have the interest in, in our ancestral town
you currently occupy, so this is a question about the village's history as
much as ours.

Any photographs, postcards or images of the farm, the barn, the green or
the church surroundings that the Council holds or knows of. Please
disclose. I have vacuumed most of Leckwith Archives already.

Any guidance on where the pre-1982 community records now sit, given that
Llandough fell within Penarth Town Council before then, and whether the
Council holds anything that came across at the 1982 reorganisation, I would
like you to please disclose.

The names of any former members, former clerks or long-standing residents
who might be willing to talk to me about the village between the 1950s and
the 1990s. I would approach anyone you suggest courteously and would not
press a refusal. Please disclose.

I am content for this email to be tabled at a meeting and minuted if the
Council wishes.
I am also happy to give a short talk to the Council or the community,
without charge, on what the records have revealed about Llandough's past —
the Roman villa, the early medieval cemetery beneath Church View Close, the
monastic history, and the farm itself.

A good deal of what I have found belongs to the village as much as my
family. Llandough just appears more committed to its current trajectory of
becoming even more of a concentration work camp, having already rejected
much of this history and heritage and native people, in lieu of whatever it
is you have underway there. I am not going to burn Llandough down to feel
its warmth. I know demonic realms are inherently ice cold. To give an
example of what I speak of, I found the Llandough Facebook page to contain
only photos of exotic takeaway foods. Sad considering its rich history and
heritage.

I am not about leading my men to spill their lifeblood on Home Office
Mahmoods and other British blades, over any of this demographic replacement
and ethnic cleansing. I am just trying to salvage, reconstruct a part of my
family's and Welsh history and heritage while people still have heads on
their shoulders here, to be able to co-operate in this matter. Even without
civil unrest, alleged fiduciaries have not kept proper records of this
case. Mine may be more complete than the British Government's and EU's at
this point. And even the Internet's, considering the heirlooms I have
inherited.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

Dear Calli,

Further to my email of 8 September 2026 concerning Great House Farm / Tŷ
Mawr, Llandough, I attach a formal schedule of the records I am seeking, so
that the request is easier for Heneb to work through and to allocate
internally. I have also completed your online enquiry form, so the request
is in your preferred channel.

I appreciate a response would not fall due until 6 October, so this is not
a chaser. It is to put the detail in one place and to clarify the basis of
the request.

On your note of 22 May. You are right that Heneb, as a limited company, is
not a public authority under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, and I do
not pursue that. Two separate points remain, and I would welcome Heneb's
position on each.

First, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 apply on a different
test — regulation 2(2) reaches bodies carrying out functions of public
administration relating to the environment, or under the control of a
public authority. If Heneb considers it falls outside that, please say so
expressly with brief reasons, so that I can direct the request elsewhere.

Second, and independently, the Historic Environment Record is a statutory
record: sections 194 and 195 of the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023
require the Welsh Ministers to maintain an HER for every local authority
area and to make it available for public inspection, and Heneb keeps the
south-east Wales record on their behalf. I therefore ask in the alternative
that this be treated as a request for access under that regime and under
Heneb's own policy.

Two things that will make this easier. If any item is too broad, please
tell me which and I will narrow it rather than have the whole request
refused. And if Heneb can supply, as a first step, simply a schedule or
index of the records it holds for this site — without copying them — that
would let me target the rest precisely and save your staff considerable
time. I am content to inspect material by appointment at Baglan or at the
HER, and any reasonable copying or staff-time charge can be notified to me
in advance for approval.

Two small administrative points. Please confirm which legal entity now
holds the records and functions formerly of Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological
Trust Ltd, and who within Heneb handles access requests of this kind.

Finally, since my correspondence in May was framed more formally: my
purpose is documentary. I am reconstructing the record of a farm my family
occupied for generations, and I would far rather do that with Heneb's help
than around it.

I should say plainly that I have read GGAT's December 1993 notification to
the Vale of Glamorgan that Condition 18 had not been complied with, and the
recommendation that a Breach of Condition Notice be issued. Whatever else
is in dispute about this site, that was the Trust doing its job properly,
and I am grateful for it.

Thank you in advance for your time in this matter,

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

MP Doughty,

Further to my letter earlier, I would like to narrow what I am kindly
asking of you, and to correct one other thing.

My letter asked which document brought the former farmhouse and garden at
Great House Farm into BP Properties Limited's registrable estate. HM Land
Registry has in fact already answered that, and I should have acknowledged
it. Its letters of 23 March and 19 April 2026 identify a conveyance dated
19 November 1982 for title WA231076, and a conveyance dated 23 May 1975 for
title WA240304. I will apply to HM Land Registry directly, on form OC2, for
copies of those deeds and their plans. I am not asking you to obtain them
for me.

Two questions remain. Both concern inconsistencies within HM Land
Registry's own correspondence, rather than anything I am asserting. So that
you need not open any attachments, I have set out the relevant passages
verbatim in the annex below, with dates and authors.

1. The 1971 abstract of title. The letter of 19 April 2026 states twice
that an abstract of title dated 1971 was lodged with the applications. The
letter of 30 July 2026 sets out a complete schedule of the documents held
on both first-registration files — thirty items for WA231076 and thirteen
for WA240304 — and no abstract of title appears anywhere on either list.
Was the abstract lodged; does the list of documents lodged (item 17 on that
schedule) record it; and if it was lodged, what became of it?

2. The conveyance of 31 December 1969. Both operative conveyances recite
the same root of title: a conveyance dated 31 December 1969 between Western
Ground Rents Limited and The British Petroleum Pension Trust Limited. That
deed does not appear on the 30 July schedule either. Was it produced to the
registry at first registration; does the list of documents lodged record
it; and if it was not produced, on what evidence was the recital accepted
as establishing the root of title?

Both questions can be answered by examining a single document which HM Land
Registry confirms it holds and describes as open to public inspection. I am
not asking it to reopen BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, to
determine ownership, or to revisit any decision it has made. A written
answer to those two questions is all I am seeking.

I can also withdraw one request from my earlier letter. I asked that the
surviving records be preserved; that is no longer necessary, as HM Land
Registry has confirmed the documents will remain on file.

My earlier request to meet you stands, but it is not pressing. These two
questions can be dealt with in writing.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

PS - see attached images. I purchased all deeds I could, but the primary
one is inaccessible for purchase as of today. I have raised this issue with
A.I.

ANNEX — VERBATIM EXTRACTS FROM HM LAND REGISTRY CORRESPONDENCE
All under reference N610CGV. Originals available on request.


A. Letter of 23 March 2026 — Lisa Griffiths, HM Land Registry Wales Office

"It appears Ty Mawr Farm was originally registered under two different
title numbers, WA231076 and WA240304. These two titles were amalgamated.
Title WA240304 was closed as a result of the amalgamation and the
registration continued under title WA231076."

"We received an application for registration on 30 Nov 1982. The
application was submitted by Linklaters & Paines of Barrington House, 59/67
Gresham Street, London, [postcode redacted], to register BP properties Limited of
Britannic House, Moor Lane, London, EC2 as proprietor. The land was
conveyed to BP Properties Limited by a Conveyance dated 19 Nov 1982 made
between (1) The British Petroleum Pension Trust Limited, (2) BP Trustees
Limited and (3) BP Properties Limited"

"We received an application for registration on 23 February 1983… The land
was conveyed to BP Properties Limited by a Conveyance dated 23 May 1975
made between (1) The British Petroleum Pension Trust Limited, (2) BP
Trustees Limited, (3) BP Properties Limited."


B. Letter of 19 April 2026 — Charlotte Takeuchi, Assistant Land Registrar
(stage one complaint response)

On the standard applied:

"In unregistered conveyancing, title is ultimately based on the estate
owner's right to be in possession of the land or to receive the rents and
profits of it. Showing a full documentary title commencing with a good root
of title that is at least 15 years old should normally establish this right
and is sufficient for land registration purposes."

On the abstract of title, in relation to WA231076:

"Our files show an abstract of title listed dated 1971 was lodged with the
application for first registration. This is effectively a summary of deeds,
documents and events which show a person's title to unregistered land."

On the abstract of title, in relation to WA240304:

"Again, our files indicate that we had sight of a copy of a 1971 abstract
of title."

On the root of title recited in the 19 November 1982 conveyance:

"The recitals clause (preamble) to that Conveyance states 'The Vendors are
seised in fee simple in the premises described in the First Schedule hereto
(hereinafter called "the premises") upon the Trusts referred to in a
Conveyance dated 31 December 1969 and made between Western Ground Rents
Limited of the one part and the Vendors of the other part..' It is clear
therefore that the applicant (BP Properties Limited) could show a good root
of title and that The British Petroleum Pension Trust acquired the land in
1969."

On the root of title recited in the 23 May 1975 conveyance:

"The recitals clause to that Conveyance states 'The Vendors are seised in
fee simple upon the trusts referred to in a conveyance dated the thirty
first day of December One thousand One hundred and sixty nine [sic] and
made between Western Ground Rents Limited of the one part and the vendors
of the other part.'"


C. Letter of 25 May 2026 — Harbinder Gill, Land Registrar (stage two, final
response)

"HM Land Registry operates a two-stage internal complaints procedure, and
this constitutes our second and final response. It is not possible to ask
anyone else in HM Land Registry to review the matter again."

"We will not be commencing the process of rectification or formally
referring the dispute."


D. Letter of 30 July 2026 — S. G. Haste, HM Land Registry Wales Office

"After an investigation of our files, we can confirm that the following
documents are available."

The letter then lists thirty documents held for title WA231076 and thirteen
for title WA240304. Item 17 of the WA231076 list reads:

"A13- DL-List of documents lodged with first registration"

Neither list includes an abstract of title of any date, nor a conveyance
dated 31 December 1969.

The letter concludes:

"We can confirm that all these documents are held on file and will remain
on file. They are all open to public inspection if require copies of them."
[sic]
texts.gm-1a0b7ad7c7c10d58:
*MP *Doughty,

Further to the correspondence from Mr Iain Banfield, and my earlier email,
I am writing again to be sure, placed on record, is the central issue which
HM Land Registry's response still does not answer.

I appreciate that HM Land Registry is not a court and that it cannot simply
reopen a Court of Appeal judgment. That, however, does not answer the
separate question of whether the land registered in 1982/83 was correctly
identified and supported by the documentary title then placed before the
Registrar.

Mr Banfield's response relies heavily upon *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler*
[1987] EWCA Civ 2. That judgment post-dated the registration by
approximately four years. It records BP Properties Ltd as having become
registered proprietor of the "whole farm" in November 1982 and then
determines the later adverse-possession dispute concerning the farmhouse
and garden. It does not, however, determine whether the 1982
first-registration application had itself correctly included the farmhouse
parcel in BP's documentary title, or whether the registration had
mistakenly conflated two historically separate parcels.

That distinction is fundamental.

My family's parcel — the former farmhouse, garden and curtilage, which I
refer to as the *House Plot* — was historically distinct from the adjoining
eastern agricultural land. The documentary history I have obtained
indicates that these areas were not simply one undifferentiated proprietary
parcel.

deposited with Glamorgan Archives in 2002 and relied on section 21 FOIA. He
subsequently retired. On the day of his retirement he directed me towards
Leckwith records and the 1939 Western Ground Rents tenancy with my
great-grandfather.

That tenancy is significant because, on the documents I have examined, it
appears to concern the eastern field rather than the House Plot containing
the farmhouse and associated buildings. I therefore do not regard that
reference as resolving the documentary position concerning Great House Farm
itself.

I need the Council to establish:

   - who is now Clerk and Proper Officer of Llandough Community Council;
   - who currently has custody of its historic minute books, correspondence
   and other records;
   - what records were handed over or inventoried when Mr Egan retired;
   - whether any search has been made specifically for Great House Farm /
   Tŷ Mawr records, rather than relying solely on the general statement that
   minute books were deposited in 2002; and
   - whether any Community Council correspondence, consultation response or
   minute relating to 89/01396/OUT or the later reserved matters survives.

If any part of this falls solely within the responsibility of Llandough
Community Council or the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales, please
identify the appropriate authority and the person to whom I should address
that part of the complaint.

   2. What the existing evidence establishes

This section turns from Community Council custody to the Vale's own
planning and archaeological file for 89/01396/OUT. The points below are
based on documents already in my possession and published archaeological
material, and are separate from the matters in Section 1, where I am asking
the Council to search its records.

   1.

   Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr is recorded in the historic environment
   record as County Treasure, reference SMR/HER 2038s / GGAT02038s, at
   approximately ST 1681 7331. The 1990 GGAT assessment records that, because
   of an ownership dispute and the subsequent sudden destruction of the
   property in 1988, the building was incompletely understood.
   2.

   Outline planning application 89/01396/OUT, submitted by BP Properties
   Ltd, followed the 1988 demolition by approximately a year. The application
   answers the relevant questions as follows: buildings to be demolished —
   "None"; site — "Disused"; previous use — "Not known".
   3.

   The Vale officer material in my possession refers to an outline-stage
   indicative scheme of 18 dwellings. The subsequent reserved-matters scheme
   approved on 3 September 1992 is for 20 dwellings.
   4.

   The 1990 evaluation recorded archaeological potential to the north of
   the churchyard and identified a medium-to-high potential area. What it does
   not establish by itself is the full extent of the archaeological remains
   subsequently encountered.
   5.

   Cotswold Archaeology excavated at the same general location in 1994,
   immediately adjacent to St Dochdwy's Church. The published archaeological
   account records 1,026 burials from an excavated area of 0.22 hectares. I am
   relying on the excavators' published figure rather than the lower secondary
   figure of 858, which appears to conflate different phases of investigation.
   6.

   PPG16 was issued in November 1990 and therefore post-dates the March
   1990 outline decision, but was applicable by the time of the September 1992
   reserved-matters decision. I am not presently asserting what archaeological
   conditions were imposed in 1992. The drawings I hold are stamped as
   approved on 3 September 1992, subject to compliance with conditions if any,
   but I do not hold the decision notice setting out the actual conditions.
   That decision notice is therefore a critical missing document.
   7.

   I am also not treating the handwritten numbering on the surviving
   consultation material as conclusively establishing which sheet relates to
   which responding body. The underlying consultation responses remain
   relevant and should be located irrespective of that numbering issue.
   8.

   The documentary gap that now needs explaining

The sequence is straightforward.

The historic farmhouse and associated buildings were demolished in December
1988.

The subsequent 1989 outline application described the site as "Disused",
stated that there were "None" buildings to be demolished, and gave the
previous use as "Not known".

The 1990 archaeological evaluation had already identified significant
archaeological potential near the churchyard.

The 1992 reserved-matters approval provided for 20 dwellings.

The 1994 excavation subsequently recorded 1,026 burials from 0.22 hectares
immediately adjacent to the church.

What I cannot establish from the records presently available to me is how
the archaeological excavation area relates spatially to the approved
housing layout and retained areas. In particular, I need the 1994
excavation plan and the corresponding Ideal Homes layout so that the two
can be compared accurately.

I also need to understand how the 1989 application descriptions came to be
accepted against the documentary and historic-environment information
already available concerning the demolished farmhouse.

I am not asking the Council to adopt my interpretation of these matters. I
am asking it to establish what was known, what was checked, what was
recorded, and what records still exist.

   4. Specific information and records requested

Please provide a substantive written response to each of the following:

   1.

   Who is currently Clerk and Proper Officer of Llandough Community
   Council, and who has custody of its historic records?
   2.

   Was Llandough Community Council consulted on application 89/01396/OUT
   and/or the subsequent reserved-matters application? If so, please provide
   the consultation requests, replies, minutes and associated correspondence,
   or confirm specifically that no such material is held.
   3.

   Please provide the full planning decision notice dated 3 September 1992,
   including all conditions, rather than the approved drawings alone.
   4.

   Please confirm whether Vale holds the 1994 Cotswold Archaeology
   site/excavation plans and the relevant Ideal Homes development layout
   plans. Please also confirm whether the Council has ever undertaken or
   commissioned a plan-to-plan comparison showing the excavation area against
   the approved development footprint.
   5.

   Please identify the officer or officers responsible for assessing the
   1989 application against the information then available concerning the 1988
   demolition and HER/SMR record 2038s, including the entries "None",
   "Disused" and "Not known".
   6.

   Please confirm what planning, enforcement, conservation/heritage,
   archaeological, consultation, photographic and correspondence records
   remain for the site and where they are presently held.
   7.

   Given the issues raised by my FOI/EIR correspondence and the corporate
   complaint of 17 September 2026, please ensure that surviving records
   concerning Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, including Community Council records
   where they remain identifiable, are preserved pending resolution of these
   matters. I am particularly concerned that records should not disappear
   simply because responsibility has passed from one office-holder to another.
   8.

   Please confirm whether there was a formal handover, inventory or records
   transfer when Mr Egan retired, and whether any such documentation records
   the location of material concerning Great House Farm, planning
   consultations, or the 1988 demolition.
   9.

   Finally, if the Council considers that any aspect concerning Mr Egan's
   conduct as Community Council Clerk falls outside the Vale's jurisdiction,
   please identify the proper route and responsible body rather than simply
   closing that part of the complaint.

I am deliberately separating evidence from inference. I am not alleging
that Mr Egan's retirement was caused by my FOI requests, nor am I alleging
that any individual deliberately concealed records. The timing, however, is
sufficiently relevant that the Council should establish what happened to
the records at the point responsibility changed. The immediate issue is
capable of being answered objectively: what records exist, what was known
to the authority, what checks were carried out, what decisions were made,
and where the missing documents are now.

Please treat this as a formal request for a written governance/records
response and address each numbered question individually. It should be read
alongside FOI/EIR reference 00210772 and my correspondence of 17–18
September 2026.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

Mr Wigley,
I am writing to make a formal complaint to Cadw concerning the handling and substantive response to my correspondence regarding Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, and particularly Cadw's 1988 consideration of whether the building should
 be protected by listing.
I am making this complaint directly to Cadw at this stage because I consider that Cadw should be given a proper opportunity to review and address the matters before any escalation to the wider Welsh Government complaints process.
For the avoidance of doubt, I am not making a further Freedom of Information request and I am not simply asking Cadw to produce records which it has already said no longer exist. I accept that Cadw has stated that all records it currently
 holds concerning the 1988 listing decision have been released.
My complaint concerns what can properly be established from the surviving evidence, whether the responses I have received have adequately addressed that evidence, and whether the historical record can now be described accurately where the underlying file
 has been lost.
1. The newly identified 1982 evidence
I have now identified a 1 October 1982 consultation letter from the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust concerning the East Vale Local Plan and the proposed Ty Maw Farm site, identified as
H2.1.
The letter states:

“Ty Maw Farm (H2.1) is designated as a three-acre residential site. As you will see from the enclosed information the settlement at Llandough developed considerably from farming and fishing... Recent excavations at Llandough by the Trust revealed early occupation,
 part of the villa and medieval grange buildings. There remains a possibility that occupation continues to the north of the church; provision should be made, therefore, for thorough investigative work prior to the development.”

I do not suggest that this document, by itself, establishes that the standing farmhouse was required to be listed.
Its significance is narrower and more demonstrable: six years before the 1988 demolition, the archaeological and planning system already contained site-specific information identifying Ty Maw Farm as a proposed development site and recording substantial
 archaeological sensitivity in the immediate Llandough area, including possible continued occupation north of the church.
That materially affects the historical context in which Cadw's 1988 assessment needs to be understood.
I therefore ask Cadw to address:


Whether this 1982 information was held by, available to, or capable of being obtained by Cadw in the period leading to the 1988 decision.

Whether Cadw has any surviving evidence showing what archaeological, planning or historic-building information was available to the inspectors or decision-makers in 1988.

Whether there was communication between Cadw and the relevant planning/archaeological authorities concerning the proposed development of Ty Maw Farm and the need for investigation or protection.

If it is no longer possible to establish whether this evidence was actually considered, whether Cadw will expressly acknowledge that uncertainty rather than treating the absence of the historic file as evidence that the relevant information was absent.

2. The 1974 RCAHMW survey
I have previously drawn Cadw's attention to the 26 April 1974 Royal Commission survey by H.J. Thomas at ST16817331.
That survey recorded Great House Farm as a historic building, including features such as the late seventeenth-century character of the house, its cross-passage arrangement, adze-worked beams, ogee stops and barrel-vaulted cellar.
Cadw has stated that only two photographs from its relevant historic material survive and that it cannot now establish whether the 1974 survey was taken into account in the 1988 listing consideration.
I accept that this may now be incapable of being proved from the surviving file.
However, there is an important distinction between:
“Cadw cannot now establish whether the information was considered”
and
“there is no evidence that the information was available or relevant.”
The surviving RCAHMW material demonstrates that professional historic-building recording existed well before the 1988 decision.
I therefore ask Cadw to address specifically whether that material was available to Cadw through the inter-agency heritage system at the time and, if so, what can now be established about its availability.
3. Cadw's own evidence that listing was actively being considered in 1988
The surviving contemporary material indicates that in December 1988 Cadw was actively considering emergency protection/spot-listing of Great House Farm, including inspection and consultation concerning the building's historic significance.
That is important because it demonstrates that this was not retrospectively invented as a heritage issue decades later. Cadw itself was considering protection immediately before the building was demolished.
Cadw's present position is that the historical listing file no longer survives and that its retention arrangements at the time cannot now be established with certainty.
I am not asking Cadw to speculate about what a destroyed file contained.
I am asking Cadw to distinguish clearly between:

what the surviving evidence positively establishes;what information was demonstrably available by 1988;what actions by Cadw in 1988 can still be established;what cannot now be established because the historic record has been lost; andany conclusions Cadw considers cannot responsibly be drawn.
That distinction is particularly important when assessing whether the surviving record provides a sufficiently reliable account of what happened.
4. The planning authority and temporary protection
I also wish to clarify the position concerning temporary protection.
I am not suggesting that Cadw itself necessarily possessed the statutory power to serve a Building Preservation Notice. I understand that such protection was a matter for the relevant local planning authority under the legislation then in force.
The question for Cadw is therefore whether, during the 1988 consideration, 
Cadw advised, discussed or communicated with the relevant planning authority concerning any available temporary protection mechanism or the need to prevent demolition pending consideration of listing.
If Cadw cannot establish what was discussed because the records no longer survive, that should be stated expressly.
5. The later description of Great House Farm as “a listed building”
I have also identified later archaeological/planning documentation in which the former site is described in terms including:

“The site formerly contained Great House Farm (a listed building).”

I am not asserting that this wording conclusively proves that Great House Farm was formally listed at that time.
I am asking Cadw to explain, insofar as the surviving evidence permits, whether there is any known provenance for that description and whether Cadw considers it accurate, erroneous, or simply impossible now to determine.
This is relevant because it illustrates the existence of potentially conflicting historical accounts concerning the building's protection status.
6. The significance of the loss of the 1988 record
Cadw has understandably stated that the historic file cannot now be produced.
However, the loss of that file creates a historical evidential limitation; it should not automatically resolve questions arising from the surviving evidence in Cadw's favour.
The appropriate conclusion may simply be that some aspects of the 1988 decision
cannot now be reconstructed with certainty.
I would therefore like Cadw to consider whether its previous responses have drawn that distinction sufficiently clearly.
7. What I am asking Cadw to do
I am asking Cadw to treat this as a formal complaint and provide a substantive response addressing the following:
A. Whether the newly identified 1982 GGAT evidence materially changes Cadw's understanding of the information environment surrounding Ty Maw Farm before the 1988 demolition.
B. Whether Cadw can establish that the 1974 RCAHMW survey was available to it in 1988.
C. Whether Cadw can establish what archaeological, planning and historic-building information was available to its officers when the building was being considered for protection.
D. What can now be established about Cadw's communications with the local planning authority and other heritage bodies during the 1988 listing consideration.
E. Whether temporary protection was discussed or advised upon and, if not capable of being established, whether Cadw will state that plainly.
F. What can be established about the inspection of Great House Farm and the ultimate listing decision.
G. Whether Cadw accepts that the loss of the historic file means that some aspects of the 1988 decision can no longer be reconstructed reliably.
H. Whether Cadw considers the surviving documentary evidence, including the 1974 survey and 1982 archaeological/planning evidence, should be reflected in any relevant contemporary heritage record or historical account.
I. Whether Cadw can explain the provenance, insofar as it is capable of doing so, of the later description of the former site as containing “a listed building.”
J. Whether Cadw considers that its previous responses have adequately distinguished between the absence of surviving evidence and evidence that something did not happen.
8. Scope of this complaint
I want to be clear that I am not asking Cadw to determine my family's wider property or title claims, nor am I asking Cadw to reach a predetermined conclusion about the historical ownership of the land.
Those matters are separate.
This complaint is confined to Cadw's own heritage-related role, the 1988 protection/listing process, the information that can now be established as having existed, and the adequacy and accuracy of Cadw's present explanation of that history.
I am also not asking Cadw to speculate about missing documents. On the contrary, I ask that the absence of those documents be treated as an evidential limitation and expressly identified as such.
9. Requested outcome
I would like Cadw to:


Register this as a formal complaint and provide a complaint reference.

Have the matter reviewed by an appropriate person who has not simply repeated the previous FOI position.

Provide a point-by-point response to the matters above, taking account of the newly identified 1982 evidence.

Correct or clarify any part of Cadw's previous correspondence that is found to have been incomplete, inaccurate or insufficiently qualified.

State clearly which matters can now be established, which cannot, and which remain uncertain because the historical records no longer survive.

I regard that as a proportionate and reasonable opportunity for Cadw to address the matter directly before I consider whether escalation through the Welsh Government complaints process is necessary.
Yours sincerely,

texts.gm-1a0b0dac48ca3d12:
Mr Wigley,

I am writing to make a *formal complaint to Cadw* concerning the handling
and substantive response to my correspondence regarding Great House Farm
(Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, and particularly Cadw's 1988 consideration of whether
the building should be protected by listing.

I am making this complaint directly to Cadw at this stage because I
consider that Cadw should be given a proper opportunity to review and
address the matters before any escalation to the wider Welsh Government
complaints process.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am *not making a further Freedom of
Information request* and I am not simply asking Cadw to produce records
which it has already said no longer exist. I accept that Cadw has stated
that all records it currently holds concerning the 1988 listing decision
have been released.

My complaint concerns what can properly be established from the surviving
evidence, whether the responses I have received have adequately addressed
that evidence, and whether the historical record can now be described
accurately where the underlying file has been lost.
1. The newly identified 1982 evidence

I have now identified a 1 October 1982 consultation letter from the
Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust concerning the East Vale Local Plan
and the proposed Ty Maw Farm site, identified as *H2.1*.

The letter states:

“Ty Maw Farm (H2.1) is designated as a three-acre residential site. As you
will see from the enclosed information the settlement at Llandough
developed considerably from farming and fishing... Recent excavations at
Llandough by the Trust revealed early occupation, part of the villa and
medieval grange buildings. There remains a possibility that occupation
continues to the north of the church; provision should be made, therefore,
for thorough investigative work prior to the development.”

I do not suggest that this document, by itself, establishes that the
standing farmhouse was required to be listed.

Its significance is narrower and more demonstrable: *six years before the
1988 demolition, the archaeological and planning system already contained
site-specific information identifying Ty Maw Farm as a proposed development
site and recording substantial archaeological sensitivity in the immediate
Llandough area, including possible continued occupation north of the
church.*

That materially affects the historical context in which Cadw's 1988
assessment needs to be understood.

I therefore ask Cadw to address:

   1.

   Whether this 1982 information was held by, available to, or capable of
   being obtained by Cadw in the period leading to the 1988 decision.
   2.

   Whether Cadw has any surviving evidence showing what archaeological,
   planning or historic-building information was available to the inspectors
   or decision-makers in 1988.
   3.

   Whether there was communication between Cadw and the relevant
   planning/archaeological authorities concerning the proposed development of
   Ty Maw Farm and the need for investigation or protection.
   4.

   If it is no longer possible to establish whether this evidence was
   actually considered, whether Cadw will expressly acknowledge that
   uncertainty rather than treating the absence of the historic file as
   evidence that the relevant information was absent.

2. The 1974 RCAHMW survey

I have previously drawn Cadw's attention to the 26 April 1974 Royal
Commission survey by H.J. Thomas at ST16817331.

That survey recorded Great House Farm as a historic building, including
features such as the late seventeenth-century character of the house, its
cross-passage arrangement, adze-worked beams, ogee stops and barrel-vaulted
cellar.

Cadw has stated that only two photographs from its relevant historic
material survive and that it cannot now establish whether the 1974 survey
was taken into account in the 1988 listing consideration.

I accept that this may now be incapable of being proved from the surviving
file.

However, there is an important distinction between:

*“Cadw cannot now establish whether the information was considered”*

and

*“there is no evidence that the information was available or relevant.”*

The surviving RCAHMW material demonstrates that professional
historic-building recording existed well before the 1988 decision.

I therefore ask Cadw to address specifically whether that material was
available to Cadw through the inter-agency heritage system at the time and,
if so, what can now be established about its availability.
3. Cadw's own evidence that listing was actively being considered in 1988

The surviving contemporary material indicates that in December 1988 Cadw
was actively considering emergency protection/spot-listing of Great House
Farm, including inspection and consultation concerning the building's
historic significance.

That is important because it demonstrates that this was not retrospectively
invented as a heritage issue decades later. Cadw itself was considering
protection immediately before the building was demolished.

Cadw's present position is that the historical listing file no longer
survives and that its retention arrangements at the time cannot now be
established with certainty.

I am not asking Cadw to speculate about what a destroyed file contained.

I am asking Cadw to distinguish clearly between:

   - what the surviving evidence positively establishes;
   - what information was demonstrably available by 1988;
   - what actions by Cadw in 1988 can still be established;
   - what cannot now be established because the historic record has been
   lost; and
   - any conclusions Cadw considers cannot responsibly be drawn.

That distinction is particularly important when assessing whether the
surviving record provides a sufficiently reliable account of what happened.
4. The planning authority and temporary protection

I also wish to clarify the position concerning temporary protection.

I am not suggesting that Cadw itself necessarily possessed the statutory
power to serve a Building Preservation Notice. I understand that such
protection was a matter for the relevant local planning authority under the
legislation then in force.

The question for Cadw is therefore whether, during the 1988
consideration, *Cadw
advised, discussed or communicated with the relevant planning authority
concerning any available temporary protection mechanism or the need to
prevent demolition pending consideration of listing.*

If Cadw cannot establish what was discussed because the records no longer
survive, that should be stated expressly.
5. The later description of Great House Farm as “a listed building”

I have also identified later archaeological/planning documentation in which
the former site is described in terms including:

“The site formerly contained Great House Farm (a listed building).”

I am not asserting that this wording conclusively proves that Great House
Farm was formally listed at that time.

I am asking Cadw to explain, insofar as the surviving evidence permits,
whether there is any known provenance for that description and whether Cadw
considers it accurate, erroneous, or simply impossible now to determine.

This is relevant because it illustrates the existence of potentially
conflicting historical accounts concerning the building's protection status.
6. The significance of the loss of the 1988 record

Cadw has understandably stated that the historic file cannot now be
produced.

However, the loss of that file creates a historical evidential limitation;
it should not automatically resolve questions arising from the surviving
evidence in Cadw's favour.

The appropriate conclusion may simply be that some aspects of the 1988
decision *cannot now be reconstructed with certainty*.

I would therefore like Cadw to consider whether its previous responses have
drawn that distinction sufficiently clearly.
7. What I am asking Cadw to do

I am asking Cadw to treat this as a formal complaint and provide a
substantive response addressing the following:

*A.* Whether the newly identified 1982 GGAT evidence materially changes
Cadw's understanding of the information environment surrounding Ty Maw Farm
before the 1988 demolition.

*B.* Whether Cadw can establish that the 1974 RCAHMW survey was available
to it in 1988.

*C.* Whether Cadw can establish what archaeological, planning and
historic-building information was available to its officers when the
building was being considered for protection.

*D.* What can now be established about Cadw's communications with the local
planning authority and other heritage bodies during the 1988 listing
consideration.

*E.* Whether temporary protection was discussed or advised upon and, if not
capable of being established, whether Cadw will state that plainly.

*F.* What can be established about the inspection of Great House Farm and
the ultimate listing decision.

*G.* Whether Cadw accepts that the loss of the historic file means that
some aspects of the 1988 decision can no longer be reconstructed reliably.

*H.* Whether Cadw considers the surviving documentary evidence, including
the 1974 survey and 1982 archaeological/planning evidence, should be
reflected in any relevant contemporary heritage record or historical
account.

*I.* Whether Cadw can explain the provenance, insofar as it is capable of
doing so, of the later description of the former site as containing “a
listed building.”

*J.* Whether Cadw considers that its previous responses have adequately
distinguished between the absence of surviving evidence and evidence that
something did not happen.
8. Scope of this complaint

I want to be clear that I am not asking Cadw to determine my family's wider
property or title claims, nor am I asking Cadw to reach a predetermined
conclusion about the historical ownership of the land.

Those matters are separate.

This complaint is confined to *Cadw's own heritage-related role, the 1988
protection/listing process, the information that can now be established as
having existed, and the adequacy and accuracy of Cadw's present explanation
of that history.*

I am also not asking Cadw to speculate about missing documents. On the
contrary, I ask that the absence of those documents be treated as an
evidential limitation and expressly identified as such.
9. Requested outcome

I would like Cadw to:

   1.

   Register this as a formal complaint and provide a complaint reference.
   2.

   Have the matter reviewed by an appropriate person who has not simply
   repeated the previous FOI position.
   3.

   Provide a point-by-point response to the matters above, taking account
   of the newly identified 1982 evidence.
   4.

   Correct or clarify any part of Cadw's previous correspondence that is
   found to have been incomplete, inaccurate or insufficiently qualified.
   5.

   State clearly which matters can now be established, which cannot, and
   which remain uncertain because the historical records no longer survive.

I regard that as a proportionate and reasonable opportunity for Cadw to
address the matter directly before I consider whether escalation through
the Welsh Government complaints process is necessary.

Yours sincerely,

*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*

Haidee,

Thanks.

I am also asking the Senedd to consider whether the circumstances
surrounding the demolition of Great House Farm, Llandough-juxta-Penarth,
and the subsequent planning and heritage history of the site warrant
independent scrutiny and, ultimately, a public inquiry or Senedd committee
inquiry.

I am not asking the Senedd to determine a private property dispute or to
decide legal questions that properly belong before the courts. My concern
is the conduct, decision-making, record-keeping and accountability of
public bodies responsible for heritage protection, planning and local
government.

The surviving evidence presents a series of unusually important questions.

Great House Farm was professionally surveyed by the Royal Commission on the
Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales in 1974. In December 1988, Cadw
was considering the building for emergency spot-listing, with a
contemporary report stating that inspectors were due to visit and consider
the case. The European Commission of Human Rights records that the
Convention application had been introduced on 3 May 1988; BP obtained
possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December 1988; and
the application was not registered by the Commission until 12 December 1988.

The evidence therefore establishes a very compressed sequence in which
emergency heritage protection was being considered, domestic interim relief
was refused, possession was obtained and the building was then destroyed
within days.

That chronology does not, by itself, establish coordination, deliberate
suppression or unlawful conduct. It does, however, warrant investigation.

There are several specific questions which I believe require answers from
an authority independent of the present local authority:

   1.

   What information and records were actually considered by Cadw when the
   1988 spot-listing decision was made?
   2.

   Was the 1974 RCAHMW architectural survey considered, and if not, why not?
   3.

   What communications took place between Cadw, South Glamorgan County
   Council, BP Properties Ltd, the courts and any other public bodies during
   the critical period immediately preceding demolition?
   4.

   What consideration was given by the local planning authority to the
   available statutory powers of preservation in circumstances where
   demolition was imminent?
   5.

   Why was the building destroyed before there could be an independent
   retrospective architectural examination of the fabric?
   6.

   How should the later archaeological evidence, including the discovery of
   approximately 1,026 burials in 1994, be understood in assessing the
   historic significance of the site and the adequacy of the earlier
   decision-making? I recognise that this later discovery cannot
   retrospectively prove that the 1988 listing decision was unlawful.
   7.

   A 1989 planning document appears to describe the site as having formerly
   contained Great House Farm “(a listed building)”. I ask that this apparent
   discrepancy be investigated and reconciled with the 1988 Cadw decision.
   8.

   What records relating to these decisions still exist, where are they
   held, and have reasonable steps been taken to preserve and disclose them?

I am particularly concerned that the destruction of the physical building
in December 1988 permanently removed primary architectural evidence which
could otherwise have been examined independently.

I also ask the Senedd to consider the wider public-interest question:
whether the present mechanisms for accountability are adequate where a
historic building is destroyed during a period of rapidly developing legal,
planning and heritage proceedings and significant questions remain about
what information was available to decision-makers.

I would therefore ask the Petitions Committee to consider accepting a
petition on this subject and, where appropriate, referring the matter to
the relevant Senedd committee or committees for investigation. I would also
welcome consideration of whether an independent public inquiry, committee
inquiry or other form of external investigation would be appropriate.

I am prepared to provide the underlying documents, chronology, court
material, heritage records, planning documents and correspondence
supporting these questions.

I am not asking the Senedd to adopt my conclusions. I am asking that the
evidence and unanswered questions be examined independently and that the
relevant public bodies be required to account for what they did, what they
knew, and what records exist.

Please confirm the appropriate route for submitting this formally to the
Senedd and whether the material can be referred to the Petitions Committee
for consideration.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Customer Relations / Planning Complaints Officer,

I wish to make a formal complaint concerning the Vale of Glamorgan
Council's Dear Customer Relations / Planning Complaints Officer,

I wish to make a formal complaint concerning the Vale of Glamorgan
Council's handling of Great House Farm, Llandough-juxta-Penarth,
particularly the circumstances surrounding its demolition in December 1988
and the subsequent planning process.


Please register this as a formal complaint under the Council's corporate
complaints procedure and provide me with a complaint reference number.


This complaint concerns the Council's administration and exercise of its
planning and heritage responsibilities. It is not intended to constitute an
appeal against a properly made historic planning decision.


1. Great House Farm, Llandough (Cardiff not Cowbridge) was recognised as a
building of historic importance


The planning and archaeological documentation concerning the site
identifies Great House Farm as a building of heritage significance.


In particular, the archaeological material identifies the former building
as a "county treasure" associated with SMR 2038s, while earlier
architectural recording by RCAHMW describes a substantial historic
farmhouse with surviving historic fabric.


The later 1990 archaeological assessment states:


«"Owing to an ownership dispute and the subsequent sudden destruction of
the property in 1988 the building was incompletely understood."»


I regard that statement as highly significant because it records,
contemporaneously with the subsequent planning process, that the building
had been destroyed suddenly and that its archaeological and architectural
history had therefore not been adequately understood or recorded.


2. The Council's apparent failure to take protective action before the 1988
demolition


I ask the Council to investigate what action, if any, its planning and
heritage officers took when Great House Farm was at risk of demolition.


In particular, I ask the Council to establish:


1. Whether the Council knew that Great House Farm was at risk of demolition
before December 1988.

2. Whether the Council received any notification, complaint, application,
correspondence or other warning concerning the proposed demolition.

3. Whether the building had been considered for statutory listing or other
statutory protection.

4. Whether consideration was given to the use of a Building Preservation
Notice or any other available statutory or administrative mechanism capable
of preventing or delaying demolition pending assessment.

5. Whether the Council's heritage officers, planning officers or
archaeological advisers were consulted.

6. Whether any inspection or photographic/architectural record was
undertaken immediately before or after the demolition.

7. Why, given the building's recognised historic significance, the Council
did not secure a comprehensive standing-building record before the building
was lost.


I am not asserting at this stage that a particular statutory power
necessarily had to be exercised. I am asking the Council to investigate
what powers and procedures were available in 1988 and why they were, or
were not, used in this case.


3. The "sudden destruction" of the building requires investigation


The 1990 archaeological assessment expressly attributes the incomplete
understanding of the building to its "subsequent sudden destruction ... in
1988".


I therefore ask the Council to establish from its records:


- the date on which it first became aware of the proposed or actual
demolition;

- the identity of the relevant officers;

- whether the Council received complaints or reports concerning demolition
activity;

- whether any site visit took place;

- whether any notice, warning, enforcement action, preservation action or
other intervention was considered;

- and whether the Council has retained records explaining why the
demolition was allowed to proceed.


This is particularly important because the building was subsequently
treated within the planning process as an already-cleared site.


4. The 1989 planning application appears to contain a significant
historical discrepancy


The outline planning application submitted by BP Properties Ltd in 1989
states, in the section asking which buildings were to be demolished:


«"None."»


The same application describes the site as "Disused" and the previous use
as "Not known".


This requires explanation because the application followed the demolition
of Great House Farm in December 1988 by approximately one year.


I ask the Council to investigate whether its planning officers:


- were aware of the former Great House Farm building when the 1989
application was processed;

- knew when and how it had been demolished;

- checked the accuracy of the applicant's statement that no buildings were
to be demolished;

- identified the former farmhouse in the planning history and supporting
documentation;

- and considered whether the demolition itself raised any planning,
heritage or enforcement issue requiring investigation.


I am particularly concerned that the planning process appears to have
proceeded on the basis of a cleared site without first establishing the
circumstances in which the historic building had disappeared.


5. Failure to create an adequate record of the lost building


The subsequent archaeological documentation states that the building was
"incompletely understood".


I ask the Council to explain what mitigation, recording or investigation it
required in consequence.


The documentary evidence presently available indicates that substantial
historic fabric and multiple phases of the building existed, yet the
building was destroyed without a complete standing-building survey having
been secured.


I therefore ask the Council to identify:


- all surveys undertaken before demolition;

- all surveys undertaken after demolition;

- all archaeological or architectural advice obtained by the Council;

- all photographs held by the Council;

- all correspondence concerning the building's architectural or historic
importance;

- and the Council's policy or practice in 1988 concerning the recording of
significant unlisted historic buildings at risk.


6. Subsequent planning treatment of the site


Following demolition, the planning process concentrated heavily on
below-ground archaeology, ultimately resulting in archaeological
investigation of the cemetery and associated remains.


I do not suggest that archaeological excavation was inappropriate. My
concern is that the destruction of the standing historic building appears
to have been treated as a fait accompli rather than as an event requiring
accountability and an explanation of how the Council's heritage
responsibilities had been discharged.


The later planning documentation should therefore be reviewed alongside the
records relating to the 1988 demolition.


In particular, I ask the Council to identify precisely when the planning
authority first recorded the former farmhouse as demolished and what
explanation was placed on the planning file for its loss.


7. Matters I ask the Council to investigate


Please investigate and provide a substantive response to the following
questions:


A. What did Vale of Glamorgan Council know about the impending demolition
of Great House Farm before December 1988?


B. What statutory and non-statutory heritage protections were available to
the Council at the time?


C. Were any of those mechanisms considered or discussed?


D. Were any Building Preservation Notice, listing, enforcement, urgent
works, archaeological recording or other protective measures considered?


E. Why was the building apparently destroyed without a comprehensive
standing-building survey?


F. What records does the Council hold concerning the demolition itself?


G. Why did the 1989 planning application proceed despite the recent
demolition of a building identified in the archaeological record as a
"county treasure"?


H. Why was the applicant's answer "None" given to the question concerning
buildings to be demolished, and did the Council investigate the apparent
discrepancy?


I. Did any Council officer consider whether the 1988 demolition constituted
a breach of planning control or otherwise required investigation?


J. Did the Council investigate whether the building had been demolished
lawfully?


K. What heritage assessment was undertaken before the subsequent
development permissions were processed?


L. What lessons has the Council subsequently incorporated into its
procedures for County Treasures and other locally significant historic
buildings?


8. Records requested as part of the investigation


Please preserve and review all relevant records, including planning files,
enforcement records, heritage files, committee papers, officer reports,
internal correspondence, site inspection notes, photographs, archaeological
correspondence and consultation records concerning:


- Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr / Cedfin / Cydfin;

- SMR/HER reference 2038s / GGAT02038s;

- the December 1988 demolition;

- the 1989 outline planning application;

- the 1990 archaeological assessment;

- and the subsequent reserved matters/development applications.


I would also ask that the Council identify any material which has been
destroyed or cannot now be located, together with the applicable
retention/disposal record where one exists.


9. Outcome sought


I am seeking a formal investigation and a reasoned written explanation of
the Council's actions and omissions.


In particular, I ask the Council to determine:


1. Whether its officers discharged the heritage and planning
responsibilities applicable at the time.

2. Whether any failure occurred in relation to the identification,
protection, recording or investigation of Great House Farm.

3. Whether the Council's handling of the 1989 planning application
appropriately addressed the recent demolition of the building.

4. Whether any relevant records have been lost or destroyed and, if so,
when and under what retention arrangements.

5. What procedural lessons arise from the case.


I also request disclosure of the relevant non-exempt records identified
during the complaint investigation, where these are not otherwise
available. I recognise that requests for specific recorded information may
need to be dealt with separately under the appropriate information-access
regime.


I have only recently been able to examine and correlate the surviving
planning, archaeological and heritage documentation sufficiently to
identify these issues. I therefore ask that the Council accepts the
complaint for investigation notwithstanding the age of the events concerned.


Please acknowledge receipt and confirm the complaint reference and the
officer responsible for its investigation.


Yours faithfully,

Dear NMR / RCAHMW cataloguing team,

Please could you check whether Emergency Recording case RCS2/1/1777 is correctly assigned.

The Coflein description reads:

Great House (Ty Mawr), Bonvilston – measured drawings, copies of historic maps, photographic material description and location plan received in the course of Emergency Recording case RCS2/1/1777, filed in nprn order.

There are two distinct Vale of Glamorgan sites with that name:

1. Ty Mawr / Great House, Bonvilston – still standing, Grade II (Cadw 13603), south side of the A48 opposite St Mary’s Church.

2. Great House Farm, Llandough (near Penarth) – NPRN 20182, ST1681073310, demolished 6 December 1988. RCAHMW already holds NMR Site Files for it (plan with additions dated 12/12/1988; Suggett account; press cuttings).

Emergency Recording of measured drawings, historic maps and photographs is the pattern one would expect for the Llandough demolition, not for the surviving Bonvilston house. Adjacent ERC case RCS2/1/1776 is also of that period.

Happy to supply further identifiers if useful.

Regards,

Sion Buckler
