Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for information about Llandough Primary School and your further enquires around whom you within the Information Governance team you have been corresponding with.

You asked

Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, where applicable, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004, I request copies of records relating to the acquisition of the land used for the construction of Llandough Primary School.

Specifically, I request:

■ The transfer deed, conveyance or other legal instrument by which the Council acquired the land.

■ The purchase price or consideration paid for the land.

■ If the land was gifted, transferred at nominal value or below market value, records explaining the basis for that arrangement.

■ Any valuation reports obtained before acquisition.

■ Any agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP (or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company) concerning the transfer of the land.

■ Any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports authorising the acquisition.

■ Any planning agreements or obligations connected with the transfer.

If any of the requested information is already publicly available, please provide the relevant links or document references.

You then issued further correspondence requesting:

On 14 July 2026 you acknowledged my FOI/EIR request (Case Ref 00211027) concerning the acquisition of land for Llandough Primary School.

I replied the same day asking for the name of the officer who sent the acknowledgement. I have received no further response or substantive reply.

Our Response

The transfer deed, conveyance or other legal instrument by which the Council acquired the land
The Council holds a conveyance dated 11 June 1965 made between:
1.            Lakeside and Llandough Development Company Limited;
2.            Western Ground Rents Limited; and
3.            The Glamorgan County Council.
A scanned copy of the conveyance and its plan is attached (“the 1965 Conveyance”).

The purchase price or consideration paid for the land
The consideration recorded in the 1965 Conveyance is £16,800.

If the land was gifted, transferred at nominal value or below market value, records explaining the basis of that arrangement
The 1965 Conveyance records a purchase for £16,800. No record has been located within the papers held by Legal Services indicating that the land was gifted or transferred at nominal value or below market value.

Any valuation reports obtained before acquisition
Searches were undertaken with Legal Services and Estates Department. No valuation report relating to the acquisition has been identified. The Council does not hold any valuation report falling within the scope of this request.

Any agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP, or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company, concerning the transfer
No agreements, correspondence or meeting minutes between the Council and BP or any BP subsidiary, trust or associated company relating to the acquisition of the land have been identified.

Any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports authorising the acquisition
The Council has not identified any Cabinet, Committee or Council reports within its current records management systems which fall within the scope of your request. Given the age of the acquisition, any surviving historic records may have been transferred to Glamorgan Archives. You may wish to contact Glamorgan Archives directly regarding records from this period.

Any planning agreements or obligations connected with the transfer
No planning agreement or planning obligation connected with the 1965 Conveyance has been identified within the title deeds held by Legal Services or, within the Planning Departments records.

We have considered this aspect of your correspondence under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.
The Council’s Information Governance Team deal with requests on a collective basis and all requests will be considered by different officers. The requests are dealt with via a generic e-mail account so that all officers in the Team can consider correspondence.  There are several reasons why the Information Governance Team work in this way.  One reason is to ensure that correspondence is considered as soon as possible and to ensure that messages or e-mails are not sent to individuals and overlooked within our systems overall.  The information requested is also considered to constitute the personal data of a member of staff and disclosure would amount to disclosure to the world at large. Therefore the Council is unable to provide the name of the individual officer, because it is not considered that there is a lawful basis that would make disclosure fair or necessary in the circumstances.  The Council's correspondence is issued on behalf of the authority, and requests for information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 or the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 are made to the Council as a public authority rather than to individual officers. It is not necessary to know the identity of a particular officer in order to submit a valid request for information.

Sirs/Ma'am,

I have been liaising a lot with local authorities in South Wales the last
year regarding my interest in Llandough.

This is a line of enquiry I wish to open about a separate matter. I am
writing on behalf of a US-based company to explore the possibility of
establishing a unique satellite office in South Wales.

The interest is in discussing a potential Commercial Guardianship Tenancy
or alternative lease arrangement for Lavernock Battery and Fort.

I understand that management and ownership of the site involve multiple
stakeholders, and I am reaching out to gauge your initial interest in such
an arrangement.

This proposal is a scenario that solves a common issue for this heritage
and coastal site—preventing dereliction, vandalism, and weathering through
active, professional occupation.

## Why a Commercial Guardianship?
Rather than a traditional commercial takeover, the type of agreement would
have a responsible custodians on site. Guardianship tenancies are not new
to Councils in Wales.

Occupancy would provide:

* Active Security & Maintenance: A regular physical presence on-site to
deter anti-social behavior and immediately flag structural or environmental
issues.

* Preservation of Heritage: respect the Scheduled Ancient Monument status
of the structures. Any workspace configuration would be entirely
low-impact, fully reversible, and designed to protect the historical
integrity of the architecture.

* Sympathetic Integration: mindful of the surrounding Lavernock Point
Nature Reserve and local businesses. Small team to operate quietly,
ensuring zero disruption to local wildlife, public footpaths, or
neighboring holiday operations.

I believe that breathing new life into these historic structures through a
controlled, professional occupancy could be an excellent model for
sustainable heritage preservation.

I welcome the opportunity to discuss this concept with you and my US
business associates, to see if a mutual arrangement could be reached. Could
you please let me know if this is a proposal your organisations would be
open to exploring?

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Warm regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

The published citations which identify RCAHMW as the source, and which state that the objects are at the National Museum of Wales, are:

Dear FOI Team,

Thank you for the internal review outcome dated 8 September 2026.

I note that the review upholds the original decision. I do not, however,
consider that the review has answered the substantive questions raised in
my request for internal review.

I am therefore putting the position on record, while also making a separate
new request for recorded information which your review confirms already
exists.

1. Records identified during the additional searches

On 14 August 2026, Amgueddfa Cymru stated that the additional enquiries had
identified:

"some information relating generally to Great House Farm and the
surrounding area".

The internal review now describes these as:

"a small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm,
Llandough".

The wording has therefore changed slightly, but the material fact has not:
the Museum confirms that records referring to Great House Farm were
identified.

My internal-review request specifically asked for those records to be
identified and, where not exempt, provided.

The review does not do so.

Simply stating that the records are considered to fall outside categories 1
to 9 does not identify what they are, where they are held, when they were
created, or their reference numbers.

2. Archived electronic systems

My request of 14 August specifically asked:

- which archived systems were searched;
- the approximate date ranges covered;
- whether historical email or correspondence archives were searched;
- whether legacy collections-management databases were searched; and
- whether any archived systems were unavailable, incomplete or incapable of
being searched.

The review answers none of these questions individually.

Instead, it states:

"archived electronic records reasonably capable of containing information
within scope were considered"

and:

"Any data stored within a system or database pre-dating the existing
Collections Management Systems, would have been migrated into the incumbent
solution, and therefore included in the search."

The first statement describes a conclusion, rather than identifying the
systems actually searched.

The second is an assumption about migration completeness. "Would have been
migrated" is not a search result and does not establish that the relevant
historical data was in fact migrated, completely migrated, retained,
searchable and included in the particular search undertaken.

3. Correspondence independent of accessioned objects

This is the most significant issue.

The original request expressly sought correspondence and administrative
records concerning, among other things:

- identification;
- recovery;
- ownership;
- location;
- the Buckler and Williams families;
- Cardiff Council;
- Cardiff Castle;
- the Bute Estate;
- museums; and
- other public authorities.

Those categories were deliberately not restricted to objects which had
subsequently been accessioned by the Museum.

The review states:

"As no such objects were identified as having been acquired by the Museum,
no associated acquisition, provenance, ownership, loan, disposal or related
correspondence concerning such objects was identified."

That reasoning addresses correspondence attached to an identified
accessioned object. It does not establish that correspondence was searched
for independently of an accession record.

For example, an enquiry concerning an item, a communication about possible
provenance, a request to identify an object, a discussion concerning
temporary custody, a disposal enquiry, a communication with another
institution, or correspondence about the contents of a property could exist
without the item ever becoming an accessioned Museum object.

Accordingly, the fact that no accessioned object was identified does not
itself establish that no such correspondence existed or was held.

The subsequent statement:

"The review did not identify evidence that the Museum holds correspondence
concerning the identification, ownership, recovery or location of Great
House Farm furniture or household effects."

still does not establish whether the relevant correspondence repositories
were actually searched.

4. Search terms

My internal-review request set out specific terms and variants and asked
the Museum to confirm whether those terms had been used.

The review now states only:

"appropriate search terms and variants were used"

and refers generally to:

"location names, property names, family names and associated variants".

That does not confirm whether the specific terms identified in my request
were searched.

In particular, the review does not say whether searches included
combinations or variants involving:

"Bute Estate", "Bute", "Cardiff Castle", "Cardiff Council", "household
effects", "contents", "dispersal", "recovery", "transfer", "demolition",
"provenance", "ownership"

and the other terms specifically identified in my 14 August correspondence.

The distinction matters because a search for a property name or family name
is not necessarily equivalent to a search for correspondence concerning the
dispersal, recovery, transfer or ownership of its contents.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction

My request also asked what evidential basis existed for the earlier
statement that the Museum was not aware of relevant records having been
transferred to another institution or destroyed.

The review now says:

"The statement that the Museum is not aware of relevant records having been
transferred or destroyed reflects the outcome of the searches undertaken
and the knowledge of relevant collections staff."

This combines two different things: documentary searches and institutional
recollection.

It does not tell me whether the Museum searched:

- transfer or accession-out records;
- disposal records;
- retention and destruction records;
- archival transfer documentation; or
- other records capable of establishing whether material had previously
been transferred or destroyed.

There is an important distinction between:

"no record of transfer or destruction was identified in the records
searched"

and:

"there is no evidence that any transfer or destruction occurred".

The review does not make that distinction sufficiently clear.

6. Searches concerning external institutions

The original request expressly contemplated records concerning Cardiff
Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate and other external bodies.

The review states:

"Searches were not limited solely to object catalogue records."

That is helpful, but it still does not identify what non-catalogue
repositories were searched.

For example, it does not identify whether searches were made of curator
correspondence, departmental files, donor correspondence,
acquisition/disposal correspondence, provenance files, loan files,
institutional correspondence indexes, or other historical administrative
records in which communications with external institutions might have been
recorded.

Again, the issue is not whether the Museum considers the search reasonable.
It is whether the relevant classes of records were actually searched.

7. The significance of the "balance of probabilities" conclusion

I note the review's conclusion that, "on the balance of probabilities", the
Museum does not hold recorded information within the scope of the request.

I do not dispute that a negative FOI determination may ultimately be
reached on that basis.

However, the balance-of-probabilities conclusion necessarily depends upon
the quality, scope and rigour of the searches on which it is based. The
ICO's guidance states that, where a requester disputes whether relevant
information has been located, the authority should be able to provide a
reasoned and detailed account of how it determined that further information
was not held, including the areas searched, staff consulted and, for
electronic searches, the keywords, accounts and time parameters used.

My concern remains that the review repeatedly substitutes statements such
as "we are satisfied", "appropriate", "reasonably capable" and "on the
balance of probabilities" for the underlying factual information about what
was actually searched.

I therefore consider the review outcome insufficiently informative on the
specific search methodology raised in my review request.

I reserve my right to refer the handling of FOI 2026-020 and the internal
review to the Information Commissioner's Office.

Separate new FOI request

Separately from the above, I am now making a new request under the Freedom
of Information Act 2000.

This new request is deliberately limited to recorded information which your
own correspondence confirms was identified or generated in connection with
the searches already undertaken.

Please provide:

A. Records identified

The "small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm,
Llandough" identified during the additional enquiries referred to in your
email of 14 August 2026 and the internal review outcome of 8 September 2026.

For each record, please provide, where recorded:

- title or description;
- date;
- collection, series or department;
- system or repository;
- reference, accession or record number; and
- a copy of the record, subject to any applicable exemption.

If any part of a record is exempt, please identify the exemption relied
upon and provide the remainder where reasonably practicable.

Limb A is confined to the records your 14 August and 8 September letters
say were identified in the FOI 2026-020 additional enquiries. It is not a
new collection-wide search. If any of those records are also in scope of
FOI 2026-032 or FOI 2026-036, please schedule them once and cross-refer.
Please do not refuse this request as a duplicate.

the disposal or transfer authority;

the date of the action;

Critique.

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for an internal review of FOI 2026-020 concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough.

The reviewer has considered your original request, the responses provided by the Museum, the additional enquiries undertaken following your request for clarification on 3rd August 2026, and the concerns raised in your email requesting an internal review.

We are satisfied that the request was interpreted correctly and that reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken to identify information falling within the scope of the request. Following the original response, the Museum undertook additional enquiries across relevant collections records and archived electronic records in order to satisfy itself that no information had been overlooked.

We are satisfied that the searches undertaken were appropriate to the nature and scope of the request and that no further searches are required in order to determine whether Amgueddfa Cymru holds information within scope.  The review therefore upholds the original decision that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold recorded information concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough falling within categories 1 to 9 of your request.

Response to the points raised

1. Information identified concerning Great House Farm
During the additional enquiries, a small number of records referring generally to Great House Farm, Llandough were identified. These records do not relate to furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm and do not fall within categories 1 to 9 of your original request. The reviewer is therefore satisfied that they fall outside the scope of the request.

2. Scope of the archived electronic search

We are satisfied that archived electronic records reasonably capable of containing information within scope were considered as part of the searches undertaken. Any data stored within a system or database pre-dating the existing Collections Management Systems, would have been migrated into the incumbent solution, and therefore included in the search.

3. Correspondence and administrative records
The review considered whether correspondence or administrative records relating to the requested items were held.

The Museum's collections records include accession documentation and associated collection records relating to objects acquired by the Museum. Searches of those records did not identify any furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms or other movable property originating from Great House Farm.   As no such objects were identified as having been acquired by the Museum, no associated acquisition, provenance, ownership, loan, disposal or related correspondence concerning such objects was identified.

The review did not identify evidence that the Museum holds correspondence concerning the identification, ownership, recovery or location of Great House Farm furniture or household effects.

4. Search terms
We are satisfied that appropriate search terms and variants were used across the relevant collections management systems, collection records and associated documentation. These included relevant location names, property names, family names and associated variants reasonably capable of identifying records within scope.

The review is satisfied that the search methodology was reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances.

5. Transfer, disposal and destruction
The statement that the Museum is not aware of relevant records having been transferred or destroyed reflects the outcome of the searches undertaken and the knowledge of relevant collections staff.  The review did not identify any records showing that information within the scope of your request had been transferred to another institution or destroyed.

For clarity, the Museum's position is that no relevant records were identified.

6. Records concerning external institutions
We note that your request sought records concerning communications with Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle, the Bute Estate and other bodies regarding objects originating from Great House Farm. Searches were not limited solely to object catalogue records. Relevant collection documentation and associated records were also considered.

No records were identified concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques, fixtures, heirlooms, or other movable property originating from Great House Farm, including correspondence with the organisations referred to in your request.

7. Advice and assistance
The Museum does not hold information identifying a specific department, collection, archive or record series within Cardiff Council or Cardiff Castle that is likely to contain the information you seek. The advice previously provided reflected our general view that those organisations would be more likely than Amgueddfa Cymru to hold records relating to the ownership, management or disposal of property associated with Great House Farm.

Conclusion
Having considered all of the information available, we are satisfied that Amgueddfa Cymru undertook reasonable and proportionate searches and that, on the balance of probabilities, the Museum does not hold recorded information falling within the scope of your request. The original decision is therefore upheld.

If you remain dissatisfied, you have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner's Office.

Dear Sion Buckler,

Thank you for your email of 22nd August, received into our enquiries system 24th August.

To answer your points in turn:


  1.  DBDT/10/19 describes Daniel Thomas as ‘of the Town of Cardiff, Builder’.  There are no further identifying details for Daniel Thomas in the documents.  We can provide copies of the documents at a charge or they can be accessed for free in our public searchroom.  Please let us know if you would like a quote for digital copies.
  2.  There are no additional deeds described on our catalogue between Daniel or Alfred Thomas and the Bute Estate.
  3.  There are no additional records relating to quarrying in Llandough or around Ty Mawr / Great House Farm.
  4.  If you have not already got a copy of Daniel Thomas’ will, you can apply for a copy of probate from the Probate Office: Search probate records for documents and wills (England and Wales) - GOV.UK<https://www.gov.uk/search-will-probate>.
  5.  We think you have probably already covered all the material we have on this matter but…
1-3)  We do not hold the majority of the Bute Estate records.  I attach a finding aid to the Bute Estate records that are currently held by Cardiff Library. These records are soon to be transferred to us so please let us know if there is anything on this list that you are interested in.  Other records of the Bute Estate can be found at the National Library of Wales.
4)  We are not sure if you have consulted D696 which includes a book plans and rental books for land owned by Western Ground Rents Ltd c1938-1944.
6. Have you looked at historic Ordnance Survey plans to show boundaries?  Some of these can be viewed online e.g. Map Finder - with Outlines - National Library of Scotland<https://maps.nls.uk/geo/find/#zoom=15.0&lat=51.44833&lon=-3.19885&layers=101&b=1&z=0&point=51.45192,-3.19801&i=135196558>.  Mary consulted the 1910 Land Valuation book for Llandough (DVAL/1/33) but we do not have the corresponding maps to go with this – you would need to contact the National Archives for a copy of this.

We hope that this information is of use to you.  Please note that we aim to answer all emails in order but the longer more complicated ones may take up to 15 working days to respond to.

Yours sincerely,

Glamorgan Archives Team,

I am writing to make a targeted archive research enquiry concerning the DBDT collection and any related Bute, Mountjoy or Western Ground Rents material held by Glamorgan Archives.

I am investigating the historic title, occupation and parcel boundaries of Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, particularly evidence concerning a possible historical division of the farm between land retained by the Bute Estate and land allegedly sold or transferred to Daniel Thomas.

A family witness account describes a specific arrangement under which approximately ten acres, including the farmhouse, were allegedly sold by the Bute Estate to Daniel Thomas, while a separate portion of approximately nine acres remained under the Bute Estate. The account further describes quarrying on the Thomas-held land and an agreement under which the freehold would eventually pass to the occupying family when quarrying ceased.

I appreciate that this account requires verification against the original documentary record. I am therefore seeking to identify the relevant deeds, agreements, plans and subsequent title documents.

1. Verification of specific DBDT catalogue entries

Please confirm the exact property description, parties and date of the following catalogue entries, and, if possible, provide a digital copy or scan of the opening parties clause and any attached or marginal plan:

  *   DBDT10/19 – Lease (counterpart), described in the catalogue as concerning land and messuages in Bute Street, Cardiff, from trustees of the late Marquess of Bute to Mr Daniel Thomas, October 1850.
  *   DBDT10/20 – Agreement for a building lease of premises in Bute Town, Cardiff, involving the same parties, June 1849.

I understand from the catalogue descriptions that these items concern Cardiff rather than Llandough. My purpose is to establish whether the Daniel Thomas named in these instruments can be identified sufficiently to determine whether he is the same individual later connected with the Llandough lime works and land interests, or whether these are unrelated transactions involving another person of the same name.

Please also advise whether either document contains information identifying Daniel Thomas by residence, occupation, estate, trusteeship or other distinguishing details.

2. Targeted search for a Bute–Daniel Thomas transaction at or near Llandough

Please search the catalogue descriptions and indexes available to Glamorgan Archives for any deed, conveyance, exchange, sale, transfer, lease, agreement, plan or related instrument involving:

  *   Daniel Thomas;
  *   Alfred Thomas;
  *   the Marquess of Bute;
  *   trustees of the Marquess of Bute;
  *   the Bute Estate;

and land at or near:

  *   Llandough;
  *   Great House Farm / Great House / Tŷ Mawr;
  *   adjoining land or parcels that may subsequently have formed part of the farm.

I am particularly interested in transactions dating from approximately 1876 to 1878, but would be grateful for references to earlier or later documents where they form part of the same chain of title.

In particular, I am seeking evidence capable of confirming or disproving whether any defined parcel of land was conveyed by the Bute Estate to Daniel Thomas.

3. Quarrying, lime works and any conditional reversion or transfer

Please identify any relevant records concerning land at Llandough or Great House Farm that refer to:

  *   quarrying;
  *   quarries or quarry land;
  *   lime works or lime kilns;
  *   mineral rights;
  *   removal of quarrying machinery;
  *   reduction or cessation of rent as land was quarried;
  *   termination of quarrying;
  *   a future conveyance, reversion, surrender or transfer of a freehold interest when quarrying ceased.

The particular issue I am investigating is whether an agreement existed under which occupation or ownership of a defined parcel was intended to change when quarrying operations came to an end.

4. Daniel Thomas, Alfred Thomas and the Llandough lime works

Please identify any documents linking Daniel Thomas, or his son Alfred Thomas (later Lord Pontypridd), with:

  *   land at Llandough;
  *   the Llandough lime works or lime kilns;
  *   quarrying operations;
  *   Great House Farm or adjoining agricultural land;
  *   any freehold or leasehold interest in the area.

I would be particularly interested in estate papers, correspondence, conveyances, wills, probate-related estate records, rentals, rent books, abstracts of title and plans that may trace what became of any Daniel Thomas interest after his death or thereafter.

5. Subsequent title and occupation

Please identify any abstracts of title, estate maps, conveyances, correspondence, tenancy records or other material that may assist in establishing:

  1.  what happened to any freehold interest held by Daniel Thomas or his estate;
  2.  whether such an interest was ever conveyed, surrendered or transferred back to the Bute Estate or another party;
  3.  whether the Bute Estate later reacquired any relevant parcel;
  4.  whether later parties, including Mountjoy Ltd or Western Ground Rents Ltd, acquired title to land previously held by Daniel Thomas or his successors;
  5.  the basis on which later tenancies described as covering the "whole" of Great House Farm were granted.

I am also interested in any material linking these title questions with the occupation of the farm by the Williams family.

6. Plans and parcel boundaries

A separate line of research concerns the possibility that historic legal boundaries passed through or between different parts of the Great House Farm complex.

Accordingly, please identify any:

  *   estate maps;
  *   conveyance plans;
  *   tenancy plans;
  *   quarry plans;
  *   large-scale plans;
  *   boundary plans;
  *   valuation plans;

that show Great House Farm, the farmhouse, garden, stables, outbuildings or adjoining parcels.

I am particularly interested in documents that could establish whether different parts of the historic building complex fell within different legal parcels.

I appreciate that some of these requests may require staff research beyond a standard enquiry. My immediate priority is to obtain the relevant catalogue references and confirmation of what material exists. If more detailed searching or document retrieval is necessary, please let me know the applicable procedure, estimated cost and whether a formal paid research request would be required.

If relevant documents have been digitised, I would be grateful for details of the cost of obtaining copies. Otherwise, please advise whether they can be consulted in person and whether any restrictions or advance ordering requirements apply.

Thank you for your assistance. The documents identified through this enquiry may be important to reconstructing the historical chain of title and occupation of Great House Farm, Llandough from the nineteenth century onwards.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

> Sirs/Ma'am,
>
> Further to my last two emails this week, and in response to yours, which
> is appreciated, please see the attached documents.
>
> My latest version file on yourselves; CADW. And a mock application to a
> mock AI chancery court; a simulation I'm running in a karpathy autoresearch
> loop as a long horizon agent to refine the arguments my family made for the
> last century before being silenced. And spending the last 4 decades like
> hostage prisoners of war.
>
> While CADW may ultimately have played what could appear to be a relatively
> small part in the wider circumstances surrounding my family's dispossession
> of our home and land, I want that part to be fully understood, accurately
> recorded and, where necessary, properly scrutinised. Any possible
> institutional failure you might have identified isn't the ice berge here, I
> assure you. Not even the tip of it.
>
> I am not approaching this simply to apportion blame, although I am both
> horrified and furious reading into all this. I am trying to establish, as
> honestly and completely as I can, what happened, what was known at the
> time, what was recorded, what decisions were made, and whether proper care
> was exercised when it mattered.
>
> Thank you in advance for your cooperation. This may ultimately develop
> into a formal complaint, and if it does, CADW will of course be given a
> fair opportunity to respond to the concerns we identify. At this stage,
> however, I am trying to understand the full scope of what happened before
> reaching those conclusions.
>
> As my research continues, I may also be in a position to provide CADW with
> records concerning your own involvement which may not presently be readily
> apparent from your current records or understanding of the matter. I hope
> that, if that happens, they will be received in the same spirit in which I
> am providing them: to establish the historical truth.
>
> In the much wider context of my family's grievances concerning BP and the
> local authorities, and the eventual destruction of what had been described
> as a "county treasure", CADW may prove to be only a small part of the
> overall story. Nevertheless, I have also attached a draft Chancery Court
> application so that you can see the wider context of our grievance and
> understand where CADW's involvement sits within it.
>
> I believe that context is important.
>
> For 38 years, my family has lived with the consequences of what happened
> in 1988. We were portrayed publicly as little more than "squatters being
> evicted", and that description has stayed with us and shamed us ever since.
> The reality was considerably more complicated and, for my family,
> profoundly distressing. It was, in fact, the first time we had been off our
> land — land which we may even still own — since the 16th century, having
> acquired the estate in 1667.
>
> It remains a theory, but it is possible that an alternate, untold story is
> yet to be told, including that Llandough was once called Cedwyn Estate, and
> that the 1,000-year freehold for it, with 640 years left on that agreement,
> passed from Sir Herbert of Swansea to the Vaughan family and onto us, not
> Bute.
>
> Given that we occupied the manorial house for so many centuries, it is
> entirely plausible that we are the rightful holders of the freehold — and
> that the heirlooms Bute purchased from the last heirs of the Vaughan family
> did not actually include Cedwyn Estate. He nevertheless acted as though he
> did, dividing the land parcels. Developing his houses and the town etc. And
> I note things like the 1824 David Stewart survey in which our estate, being
> reduced to a home on the parcel it occupied, was recorded as Great House
> alias "Cedfin". Elsewhere Ked fin. And other variations.
>
> The same method used in 1974 with BP's licence letters was also used in
> 1955 (rendering our owner/occupier status merely permissive), and this may
> have occurred on multiple other land parcels prior to this — potentially in
> clandestine collaborations with the British State, given that 33 acres were
> carved out for the limeworks in the WWI effort, and War Ag occupied the
> land adjacent to ours in WWII. The council also absorbed our "playing
> fields" and so forth: a sort of eminent domain without our family receiving
> proper reparations (except once, in 1878). Llandough may have been the last
> of Wales to be colonised.
>
> I can tell you as a soldier. In Nicosia the indigenous Greeks and many
> Turks too, would approach the green line with old records of their land
> holding the UN occupied, even 4 decades later, and the UN would have to
> surrender those lands back to the indigenous. I draw a lot of parallels
> between this, our case and Wales' dream of devolution/ decolonisation. This
> case also might show we've been in a land market bubble and so a land
> market crash is coming. Our case isn't isolated or unique.
>
> I was a child in that house. My mother was pregnant, and the three of us
> were still young children. The people who removed us by force — following
> BP and the UK Government (synonymous at the time) after awarding themselves
> victory in their courts, (Magistrates as oppose to Chancery or before the
> Bench as a matter of equity, as should have happened on the merits of this
> case) — caused my mother's shoulder to become dislocated when she attempted
> to serve them with a High Court injunction ordering the occupiers not to
> destroy our home or remove our belongings. Despite that injunction, the
> house was ultimately destroyed and our possessions removed, including all
> our furniture, which came from Cardiff Castle, £30,000 of goods, a stone
> Roman-villa-type pillar, and so forth.
>
> The ITV coverage at the time showed some of what happened, including the
> injury to my mother, but not that she was pregnant and that three young
> children were inside. ITV, it seems, never aired that footage, and instead
> of responding to my FOI request, they quietly published it to a YouTube
> archive last year — apparently hoping that I, or my AI agents, or anyone
> else, would not notice this suppression. I also hold other ITV footage
> which they have not admitted to or disclosed, showing my younger baby
> sister held to watch the looting of our home.
>
> The MP is hesitant to respond, the Llandough councillor will not respond,
> and the longstanding Llandough clerk retired after initially trying, and
> failing, to dismiss me. I am ashamed of my nation. I served in war too, and
> left my military career with honours; I am bona fide, having also completed
> 22 years in Oath in 2024, the last 2 under the employ of the Vale of
> Glamorgan Council in adult care. The Land Registry also tried everything to
> steer me away from identifying their mistake in allowing BP to register our
> land in their name, without our ownership claim being lodged, in 1983. The
> fact that my nan — who had already spent 40 years challenging her ownership
> claim by 1983 — died within the two weeks she would have had to challenge
> BP's registration of our land in their name, is another matter requiring
> investigation.
>
> Much like my late father's sudden death at age 41, between BP's
> application and approval of housing development, his ECHR claim was
> rejected, and his appeal of the 1987 ruling was dismissed — on the grounds
> that BP's companies were treated as one and the same. Yet in the ruling
> itself, BP's companies were considered separately, meaning our challenge to
> one would not have affected the other. Outrageous. The same judge also went
> out of his way to say my nan "conceived the notion she owned" and said the
> unajudicated ownership dispute, set aside to award BP possession of our
> land, was final. Very suspect and nobody raised questions or challenged
> except our family i.e. 'Buckler vs United Kingdom' at the ECHR in 1988/89.
> Who also ruled in lieu of BP rights over ours as the owners. In 1974 the
> ownership hearing was ajourned. Ownership to this day has never been
> properly adjudicated.
>
> For us, this was not simply a "squatters being evicted" case, as was
> falsely reported in the news. It was the loss of our family home since
> 1667, and the forceful and prolonged seperation and severing of our
> connection to that land, which our family had maintained for generations
> and owned, and still appear to own in spite of who awarded themselves
> possession of it or occupy it — and perhaps not just the parcel we were on,
> but half the town of Llandough, by birthright. With 6 centuries left on
> that freehold from the Knight in 1500, to a military commander and leader
> like myself. The true title chain. All the while the occupiers operate from
> defective title. It's possible getting to me may prove more difficult than
> how my dad before me or nan before him were gotten to, as I am a military
> warfare professional of almost 3 decades now.
>
> It is otherwise difficult to explain what all we went through does to a
> family, particularly when the public account of what happened does not
> reflect the reality experienced by those of us who were inside the house at
> the time. My younger sister had nightmares when I brought this up with her.
> It's subsequently cruel to see her having to visit archieves for a 4th
> time, to try to see again what we are there to see.
>
> I therefore hope that CADW will understand why I am asking you to approach
> this matter with some care and humanity, as well as with the proper
> historical and professional scrutiny that it deserves. The non response
> from the Llandough councillor, classification of the 133 house plans on the
> council planning portal, delay from MP responding, is also an outrage. And
> clear bias towards the houses being developed on our stolen occupied land,
> by the holders of the defective title. No wonder my surviving family, of
> mainly women, aren't speaking up or out. It just horrifies me how they have
> had to live like such hostages under such terrorists. After a literal act
> of terrorism against us.
>
> I was involved in the effort in Iraq to break two SAS soldiers out of an
> Iraq prison under police guard, days before their execution. Me and a lot
> of the squadrons of soldiers I have around me to this day. I see my family
> in a similar light there, under the tyranny of this. And I am not standing
> for it. I'm only 41, I'm in full mental and physical health. I may have a

Sir/Madam,

I write to formally place before the Crown Prosecution Service evidence
concerning suspected historical fraud and related criminal conduct arising
from the dispossession and subsequent treatment of the former Great House
Farm, Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan.

I am currently investigating the matter and preparing proceedings
concerning the underlying proprietary dispute. I am also considering the
institution of a *private prosecution* in respect of any criminal offences
disclosed by the evidence.

I specifically invite the CPS to consider, at this stage, whether this is a
case in which the Director of Public Prosecutions should exercise the power
under *section 6(2) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 to take over
the conduct of a private prosecution*, should proceedings be instituted.

The principal concern is not simply the disputed ownership of land. The
historical evidence appears to disclose a possible pattern in which the
family's established occupation and proprietary position were progressively
characterised as merely permissive.

Of particular significance is the apparent treatment of the occupation in
the *1955 proceedings*, followed by the more explicit attempt in *1974* to
establish a rent-free licence arrangement concerning the property. I am
investigating whether these were independent legal positions or whether
they formed part of a longer and coordinated course of conduct intended to
create or manufacture a documentary/legal basis for treating an established
proprietary occupation as permissive, thereby facilitating the acquisition
or retention of the land.

The subsequent involvement of *BP Properties Ltd and BP Pension Trust*, the
registration of title WA231076 in 1982, and the litigation culminating in
the 1987 Court of Appeal proceedings are material to that investigation.

I do not ask the CPS to determine the civil title dispute. The question I
ask is whether the documentary sequence discloses evidence capable of
supporting criminal offences involving fraud, conspiracy, false or
misleading representations, concealment of material information, or other
offences arising from the alleged acquisition or preservation of property
rights.

I am particularly concerned that conduct occurring at different stages may
only become intelligible when examined as a single historical sequence
rather than as isolated civil proceedings. The apparent attempt to
establish permissive occupation in 1955, the subsequent licence proposal in
1974, the later registration of title, and the representations made in the
litigation may therefore warrant consideration together.

I recognise that the CPS will need sufficient evidence to apply the Full
Code Test and that the existence of a civil dispute does not itself
establish criminal conduct. I am not presenting the allegation as proved. I
am presenting the documentary evidence and asking the prosecuting authority
to determine whether it warrants criminal investigation and/or prosecution.

The CPS's published guidance confirms that a private prosecutor may ask the
CPS to take over a private prosecution and that, when specifically
requested to intervene, the CPS must make a decision whether or not to take
it over. The guidance further recognises that the CPS may take over and
continue a private prosecution where the Full Code Test is satisfied and
there is a particular need for the CPS to conduct the prosecution,
including in serious or complex cases or cases involving substantial
disclosure issues.

I therefore expressly request that the CPS:

   1.

   *Consider whether it would be prepared to take over a private
   prosecution under section 6(2) of the Prosecution of Offences Act 1985 if
   proceedings are instituted;*
   2.

   *Confirm whether the matter should instead be referred to an
   investigative authority for investigation before the CPS considers taking
   over proceedings;*
   3.

   *Identify the appropriate CPS division or office to which the evidence
   should be submitted; and*
   4.

   *If the CPS is not prepared to consider taking over such proceedings,
   expressly confirm that position and the reason for it.*

I am able to provide an indexed evidential bundle containing the relevant
1955 and 1974 material, historical conveyances and plans, Land Registry
documentation concerning WA231076, relevant court records and a chronology
identifying the specific documentary inconsistencies and matters which I
consider require investigation.

I would prefer the CPS to have the opportunity to consider the matter at
this stage rather than for a private prosecution to be commenced without
first giving the public prosecuting authority an opportunity to determine
whether it considers the case sufficiently serious, complex or otherwise
appropriate for public prosecution.

Please therefore treat this correspondence as a *formal request for
consideration of CPS involvement and potential exercise of the DPP's
section 6(2) power*, and confirm the appropriate procedure for submitting
the evidence for that purpose.

There's 133 houses approved for development on land that I believe to be
concealed sacred even holy ancient welsh woodland. And my land as
surviving, unestiguished claim and heir and successor of that claim has
been a position our family have maintain unto our suspicious and
conveniently timed deaths (my father while planning was approved for 20
houses, my nan before him in the 2 weeks she will have had to challenge BP
registering and merging our land as theirs at the land registry in 1983).
The current possessor holds defective title, in my humble estimation. And I
hold interest in the land, which is being ignored along with my concerns,
by local authories who have vested interest in the development of the
houses. The councillor for Llandough and MP both will not reply. The
council clerk retired. This is being dragged into the shadows and I suspect
clandestine warfare, silence and violence. Whereas I am trying to keep the
matter open, transparent and in the public eye as it is a matter of public
interest being a site of historic and archeological signficants I.e.
monestry, roman villa, county treasure home, medieval burials etc.

My investigation is ongoing. But I do see a  multi generational racket was
used for a land grab. And I am a military warfare professional, not just
the son of William Buckler.

Yours faithfully,

Daniel,

Thank you for your detailed response and for carrying out the further
searches.

I appreciate your confirmation that searches have been undertaken across
the available operating systems, including customer registration and
billing records and records relating to site visits and supply adjustments
or alterations.

Your response does, however, raise some further questions which I would be
grateful if you could clarify.

Most importantly, you state that following the migration to the current
billing systems in 2015:

“historical call notes, emails, webforms and other communications that may
previously have been associated with a customer or property account, were
not transferred and are therefore no longer available through our current
operating systems.”

This appears to establish that historical records of precisely the type I
am seeking may previously have existed, but were not migrated to the
current systems.

I am therefore not asking Welsh Water to speculate about what happened in
1988. I am asking whether there is any surviving documentary record
concerning the historical records themselves and their subsequent disposal
or migration.

Could you please clarify the following:

   1. *Pre-2015 records*

Were records relating to Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough held on any
legacy customer, property, works, engineering or billing system before the
2015 migration?

   2. *2015 migration*

Were historical records excluded from migration because they had already
reached their retention period, or were they excluded irrespective of their
age?

In particular, was there a defined cut-off date or retention rule
determining which historic property/account records were migrated?

   3. *Disposal*

If historic records relating to the property were destroyed or deleted
rather than migrated, is there any surviving disposal schedule, destruction
log, system-retirement record, data migration specification, audit record
or other documentation showing what categories of historical records were
removed?

   4. *Property records*

You state that you have been unable to identify surviving archived indexes,
work orders, engineer reports or other records relating to the property.

Could you please confirm whether these categories of records were
historically maintained separately from the customer billing/account
system, and whether searches were made for legacy engineering or works
records using the property name, rather than solely a modern customer
account number?

   5. *1988 supply alteration/disconnection*

I am particularly interested in whether the records show any historic
supply alteration, disconnection, meter removal, site visit, engineer
attendance, works order or instruction concerning Great House Farm during
1987–1989.

If no such records survive, please confirm whether this means:

a) no such record was ever created;
b) such records were created but subsequently destroyed under the
applicable retention policy; or
c) it is impossible to determine which of those possibilities applies
because the relevant historic records are no longer available.

   6. *Historical property/account identifiers*

If your systems retain any historic property reference, account number,
supply point reference, meter reference, works reference or other
identifier associated with Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), I would be grateful
if you could provide it. Even if the underlying records no longer survive,
such an identifier could assist in tracing the historic record elsewhere.

   7. *Records predating the current systems*

Finally, could you please confirm whether Dŵr Cymru/Welsh Water has any
central archive, historical records repository or retained legacy data from
before the 2015 system migration, and whether the searches undertaken
included those holdings?

I appreciate your statement that you cannot confirm what happened in 1988
where no records remain. I am not asking you to make such a determination
without evidence.

Rather, I am trying to establish the documentary chain: whether a record
existed, where it was held, whether it survived the transition to the
current systems, and, if not, what happened to it.

Your response has provided useful information in that respect, particularly
the confirmation that historical communications associated with
property/customer accounts were not transferred during the 2015 migration.

I would therefore be grateful if the above points could be answered so that
I can accurately record the extent and limitations of the surviving Welsh
Water records.

With regard to the £20 Guaranteed Standards Scheme payment, thank you. I am
happy to provide a forwarding address for that separately if required;
acceptance of that payment should not be taken as resolving or withdrawing
my substantive request for clarification concerning the historical records.

Regards,


Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

Hello Sion,

Thank you for your email in which you request a further review of any records relating to Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) and the disconnection which you believe took place during the 1980s.

I can see that our Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) team responded to your previous email on 13 August 2026 and advised that we hold no records relating either to yourself or the property in question.

My Review

I appreciate that your latest enquiry is intended to establish the circumstances surrounding the water supply to Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) in 1988, rather than seeking access to your personal data.

As previously advised, we have been unable to locate any records relating to the property following the searches undertaken. Our enquiries indicate that the property was demolished during the 1980s and any operational, customer or property records that may once have existed would fall well outside our retention periods and are no longer held.

As we do not hold any surviving records relating to the property, we are unable to confirm whether any request was made to disconnect the supply, who may have made such a request, whether supporting authority was provided, whether works were undertaken, or whether any associated correspondence or operational records were created.

Equally, we have been unable to identify any surviving archived indexes, work orders, engineer reports or other records relating to the property. As no records have been located, we cannot provide further information regarding the circumstances of any destruction beyond confirming that records are retained in accordance with applicable retention schedules and legal requirements.

Whilst I appreciate this may be disappointing; Welsh Water can only provide information that is currently held. We are unable to speculate on events or actions that may have occurred where no records remain available to verify them.

In response to your request for clarification regarding our retention periods, these vary depending on the type of data or information held. For example, telephone recordings are retained for 12 months, whereas account notes may be retained for significantly longer periods depending on the nature of the information.

We are generally required to retain customer correspondence for between six and seven years. During this period, correspondence may remain accessible through a customer's online account before it expires and is removed in line with the relevant retention schedule.

That said, following the migration to our current billing systems in 2015, historical call notes, emails, webforms and other communications that may previously have been associated with a customer or property account, were not transferred and are therefore no longer available through our current operating systems.

Outcome

I am sorry that we have been unable to provide the information you requested regarding the property and any actions that may have been taken in 1988. However, using the details provided, our DSAR team has been unable to locate any records relating to either the property or yourself.

For clarity, this has included searches across our available operating systems, including customer registration and billing records, as well as records relating to site visits and supply adjustments or alterations.

Lastly, I have identified that our response falls outside our 10-working day target for responding to written communications, and I would like to apologise for any inconvenience this may have caused.

To address this, a £20.00 Guaranteed Standards Scheme (GSS) payment can be paid to you. To allow this to be processed, please confirm a suitable forwarding address so that we can arrange for a cheque to be issued to you.

If you have any questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to get in touch by replying to this email, or by calling Customer Care on [phone redacted], available Monday to Friday between 9:00am and 4:00pm. Alternatively, you can contact our Billing Department on [phone redacted], available Monday to Friday between 8:00am and 6:00pm, and Saturday between 9:00am and 1:00pm.

Kind regards

Daniel
Customer Services

Secretary of State,

I write as the representative of my family, the House of Williams/Buckler,
concerning Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough — an approximately
800-year-old manorial house which we occupied continuously from 1667 until
its destruction in 1988, with me as an infant at the time, practically
still inside the house, with my pregnant mum.

It was my birthplace and our family’s home and land. And it still appears
to be our land, despite BP being awarded possession in 1987. I discovered
that the final ruling (for possession, not determination of ownership) was
based on a quiet 1983 land registry by BP of our land, in their names,
without disclosing my disabled widow pensioner’s ownership claim, who also
conveniently died in the two weeks she would have had to challenge this
registration, not that she was even made aware. It also states our
possession was adverse from 1955. But that was on a land parcel we rented
and defaulted on, to the east of ours, not the parcel our home and garden
and farm was on. Our parcel we occupied since 1667; we owned from 1928 when
we made our last payment on it. Originally an 1877 agreement which went
missing from our home in the 1940s, but even without that paper title,
having not paid since 1928, our possession and ownership would have
qualified as adverse by 1940.

Furthermore, this 1983 land registry non-contest by my nan was after 55
consecutive years of her asserting ownership, after the 1877 agreement
between Bute quarryman Daniel Thomas & Son enacted in 1928, when quarrying
completed. An agreement her statements report was stolen from our home in
the mid-1940s. Providing both the name of the thief who confessed to
stealing it and the estate agent who contracted him to do so.

It appears from my research so far that while a field we rented to the east
of our land was repossessed, for which our possession might very well have
been adverse from 1955, our land parcel was falsely and wrongfully treated
as being part of the systematic repossession of the adjacent land parcel,
which BP merged into theirs in 1983 from what I can gather.

I believe this confusion stems from the definition of “whole farm” (as
cited in the 1955 court order) which changed from two parcels of land in
the 1916 agricultural tenancy (conveyed to Western Ground Rents by the
Marquess of Bute in 1938) to one parcel of land following the enactment of
the 1877 agreement in 1928 (after 51 years of our payments, reportedly £4 a
year). Furthermore, the modern tenancy/agricultural tenancy Western Ground
Rents placed my great-grandfather into in 1939 for the land parcel to the
east of ours was, according to Leckwith archived records, only for the one
parcel to the east of ours and not both parcels.

In addition to the definition of “whole farm” being misunderstood to still
include our parcel after 1928, introducing ambiguity in the 1955 order, the
order of possession for Western Ground Rents’ land parcel to the east of
the one we owned and occupied (since 1667) also says our land parcel (home
and garden) was excluded from the order, but not because we owned it, but
because of my grandmother’s “condition (having just had a leg amputated)
and her resistance”. It does not mention her assertion of ownership. This
made our occupancy appear permissive and is what BP later tried in 1974
with their permissive occupancy licence letters. The basis of the pinnacle
of this dispute: the landmark legal case BP v Buckler 1987.

I say all this at least to defend my grandmother’s honour. After her
conveniently timed death in 1983, during the 1987 hearing in which she was
unable to defend herself, the judge took it upon himself to enter onto the
record that my grandmother “conceived the notion” she owned the farm. He
also dismissed my father’s appeal, citing that both BP companies were all
the same. But in the ruling in BP’s favour prior, the judge said “had my
nan challenged BP Pension Trust, it wouldn’t have counted as BP Properties,
the plaintiff, were a different company”. Which is not just a “heads they
win, tails we lose” procedural unfairness matter. But the legal precedent
that landmark legal case set by ruling my grandmother “accepted the
permissive occupancy and offer from BP and their licence letters in 1974,
because she didn’t expressly reject them” is firstly absurd by any sane,
reasonable person’s standards. Secondly, that 1987 case excluded a
newspaper article from 1974 whereby my nan expressly rejects, even got
1,000+ people to sign a petition against their housing development plan of
13 houses (likely on their parcel to the east, not ours as they never owned
ours) and the article reports her stating her lawyer had assured her her
ownership claim was valid. And she asserts “it’s my home”.

And further to all that, it is documented the court never ruled in 1974.
Not adjudicating ownership in the first hearing, which was adjourned. And
not ruling for possession in the second hearing in 1974, which was quashed.
Firstly because the clerk called them press when my disabled nan crawled to
court begging for an audience with the judge after forced attempts to
remove her. Including water being shut off for months, resulting in my
infant aunt having to go live with another family. And all our cows
drinking from the river and dying. The other factor is while the public and
press and family all had a victory, my nan’s lawyers, BP and the courts
quashed the case. But what they did was call to mention the offer to my
nan, and quashing it instantly before she had opportunity to respond. We
may still have the tape recording.

So it is not a case of her not responding and so she accepted. It is a case
that the decades of rejection and petition and press reports were concealed
and suppressed, along with these important facts, and the backdated licence
letters BP produced afterwards in 1974 and clandestine 1971 alteration of
our land parcel on the Ordnance Survey, and conveyance from BP Pension
Trust to Properties in 1975, and land registration in 1983, unbeknown to us
or anyone I suspect, was not meeting of the minds by a long shot. Yet was
all that was heard or considered in 1987. The 1987 case was not judged on
the merits of the case as it should not even have been held in the court it
was in. The court it was decided in was the least applicable court of them
all. A Chancery/Queen’s Bench i.e. equity court would have been the
appropriate court.

Further to even all this, an attempt was made by Western Ground Rents to
get my nan into a tenancy in 1949 too, for our plot. Which my nan expressly
rejected in lieu of her assertion of ownership. Even with our paper title
stolen prior to that attempt, having not paid since 1928 our possession,
even if adverse, would have qualified us as owners through adverse
possession by 1940 in any case.

WGR generated a possession order for our land, based on the ambiguity they
introduced into the 1955 order, which was never enforced and is the
interest they conveyed to BP in 1969, when conveying the land they
possessed east of ours. BP then altered the Ordnance Survey in 1971,
shifting the title “Ty Mawr” from the land parcel to the east onto our land
parcel. And appending “Farm” to the descriptor. Making our parcel better
fit the defective title chain being forged, in lieu of my nan’s missing
title chain. The 133 houses they are seeking to build on that land parcel,
ours (now Church View Close) was merged into, is defective. The title chain
traces back to and through us to what may be the 1,000 freehold issued by
Knight Sir Herbert to the Vaughan family in the 1500s. It is even possible
we have been playing the role of virtual freeholder on our land parcel, or
even tenant on the land east of ours. When all things considered, like the
fact we occupied the manorial house since 1667, may even make it possible
that we were and still are the rightful freeholders of Llandough Town
(formerly Cedwyn Estate), with 640 years left on that freehold. Because
Bute’s purchase of the last Vaughan heirs’ estate reportedly did not
include our Ty Mawr.

And Ty Mawr (alias Cefin (a possible attempt at Cedwyn) according to an
1824 David Stewart survey) was not just our home or land parcel, but enough
parcels to conclude the estate being half the town of Llandough. So this
all may be a lot bigger and run a lot deeper than even what I am bringing
to your attention. Our family also have bloodline connections to the
Vaughan, and so it is not just title, estate and deeds. I only focus on the
parcel we own, for which possession was awarded to BP, to begin unravelling
truths long suppressed and concealed.

In 1974 an ownership hearing did occur to adjudicate the ownership dispute,
but seeing as my nan could not present her title as it was stolen, the
hearing was adjourned. BP then tried to enforce the 1962 possession order.

So in summary: July 1974 = possession case, adjourned, never finally
decided.

September 1974 = old 1962 possession order revived.

October/November 1974 = threatened eviction stopped and warrant withdrawn.
Not licence letters, quashed hearing, but in fact because of overwhelming
court clerk, press and public support.

Another dimension of this, of which there are many, including BP Bailiffs
being undercover soldiers and/or accompanied by soldiers, allegedly even
SAS, is the abrupt demolition of our 800-year-old “county treasure” home.
4am the morning after, almost simultaneously, CADW refused to spot-list it
as Grade II, the council refused to issue a demolition stop order and our
High Court injunction preventing demolition or removal of our property (all
of our furniture from Cardiff Castle etc.) got overturned.

This surely should not have happened prior to the appeal procedure of those
decisions concluding, to say the least. More indications of Government
involvement/military operation. Which I do not just say as a military
warfare professional, but because other evidence supports it (including
recently declassified ITV coverage which may not even have aired). Along
with fraud and all the concealment, there are grounds to exercise the
clause in the Limitation Act and reopen this case.

I formally submit the accompanying CADW — Forensic Critique, Great House
Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough – Version 5.0.0 (August 2026).

I also enclose a mock application to an AI-assisted mock Chancery Court I
am working with. I have been using iterative research and legal-analysis
processes to test and refine the arguments arising from the historical
evidence, pending any formal legal proceedings on behalf of my family. I
include it not as a substitute for legal proceedings, but to give your
Office the wider context in which I am examining what happened. And an
illustration of a final single legal case which articulates my family’s
grievances. If they were not all so terrified to speak out, still now, even
after 38 years.

The CADW Forensic Critique is deliberately evidence-led. It distinguishes
between established facts, reasonable inferences and matters which cannot
presently be established because the underlying records no longer appear to
be available.

Its central concern is straightforward:

Cadw cannot presently produce sufficient surviving evidence to explain how
its December 1988 decision was reached, nor can it presently explain what
happened to the records documenting that decision.

Albeit we are still corresponding to establish the facts. In any case what
has been established thus far is particularly troubling given what happened
immediately afterwards.

In 1988, Cadw publicly stated that it was considering an appeal to the
Secretary of State for Wales to protect the building. The South Wales Echo
reported on 3 December 1988 that an inspector would visit “this weekend”
and liaise with RCAHMW.

The building was then demolished overnight on 5/6 December 1988, within
hours of the refusal and the simultaneous dismissal of a High Court
injunction.

I am therefore asking your Office to help, at the very least in this
correspondence with CADW, to establish as precisely as possible what
happened.

1. Contact between Cadw and the Welsh Office / Secretary of State

Please confirm, deny or clarify each of the following:

Whether any communication or outreach took place between Cadw, or its
predecessor functions, and the Office of the Secretary of State for Wales /
Welsh Office concerning Great House Farm during the period July–December
1988.

Whether any recommendation, briefing, submission, notification or formal
appeal concerning the protection or listing of Great House Farm was
submitted to the Secretary of State.

Whether my family, as the occupiers and asserted owners of the property,
was ever consulted, contacted or notified by Cadw or the Welsh Office
before the refusal decision of 5 December 1988.

If such communications occurred, I ask that the surviving records be
identified and disclosed.

If they did not occur, I ask that this be stated clearly.

2. What happened to the 1988 assessment records?

Cadw’s responses, including FOI ATISN 27021, the response from Amy Longford
dated 10 July 2026, the subsequent internal review, and the response from
Dr Andy Wigley dated 27 August 2026, indicate that:

only the two July 1988 photographs have been located;

no assessment file, inspector’s notes, decision record or internal
correspondence has been located;

no destruction record, transfer list, accession record or archive schedule
has been located; and

Cadw has stated that unsuccessful listing assessments were historically
retained for approximately three years before transfer or destruction under
the Public Records Act 1958.

This raises an obvious question which I hope your Office will appreciate is
important to my family:

If the records were destroyed, transferred or otherwise disposed of, where
is the record showing that this happened and under whose authority?

I therefore request the immediate production of any surviving destruction,
disposal, transfer or accession documentation relating to the Great House
Farm 1988 assessment file, including certificates, dockets, lists, database
entries, retention schedules, disposal authorities or other contemporaneous
records held by the Welsh Office, its predecessors, Cadw, or any repository
to which relevant records were transferred.

Where such a record exists, please provide its exact wording and identify,
insofar as recorded:

the file reference;

the disposal or transfer authority;

the date of the action;

the relevant retention period;

and the officer or authority responsible for authorising it.

If any residual material remains in existence, I ask that it be preserved
immediately and not destroyed, transferred or otherwise disposed of while
these matters remain under examination.

If no destruction, disposal or transfer documentation exists, I ask that
your Office confirm that expressly.

3. The unanswered questions surrounding the decision itself

I also ask your Office to address, or to require Cadw to address, the
outstanding questions identified in Part XII of the accompanying Forensic
Critique.

In particular:

Who was the decision-maker responsible for the refusal on 5 December 1988?

What was the registered file reference, title and record series?

What evidence was actually considered?

Was the 1974 RCAHMW survey (ST 16817331) considered?

Were SMR 2038/2038s and the relevant 1978–1980 GGAT reports considered?

What was the basis, authorship and status of the July 1988 “YYY” coding?

What communications took place with BP Properties or its agents, the local
planning authority, RCAHMW, GGAT or the High Court during the critical
period?

Was a Building Preservation Notice considered?

What retention and disposal schedule applied to the assessment?

What was the scheduled disposal/review date?

Who authorised disposal, if disposal occurred?

Which repositories and catalogues have been searched, including The
National Archives and historic Welsh Office records?

Do comparable unsuccessful listing assessments from 1988–1991 survive, and
if so, how were they retained?


These are not questions I ask simply because I disagree with the historical
decision.


I am trying to establish what evidence was before the decision-maker, what
process was followed, and what happened to the official record afterwards.

That distinction matters.


4. Independent verification

I therefore ask your Office to confirm whether it has searched, or will now
search, The National Archives catalogue and relevant historic Welsh Office
transfer documentation for records concerning Great House Farm.

If this has not already been done comprehensively, I ask that it be
undertaken and that Cadw be asked to undertake any corresponding searches
necessary to establish whether the missing assessment material was ever
transferred elsewhere.

I would also ask that any surviving records relating to the case be
preserved while these enquiries are ongoing.

5. Why I am asking

I appreciate that this is a historic matter.

But for my family it is not simply history.

This was our home. It was the place into which I was born, and the
destruction of the building came at the end of a much longer dispute
concerning our family’s occupation, land and property rights.

I have spent considerable time reconstructing what happened from surviving
court records, land records, archaeological evidence, newspapers, archival
material, FOI responses and contemporary documentation. I am not asking
your Office to accept every conclusion I have drawn.

I am asking for something more fundamental:

where the Government and its agencies can still establish what happened, I
ask that they do so; where the evidence no longer exists, I ask that they
say so plainly; and where the record of its disappearance should exist, I
ask that it be identified.

My family has lived with the consequences of these events for decades. I
believe that, at this stage, the least that can reasonably be expected is
openness, proper record-keeping and an honest examination of what happened.

I therefore ask that this correspondence, together with the attached CADW —
Forensic Critique v5.0.0, be treated as a formal request for recorded
information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, as well as a request
for clarification of the records-management position concerning Cadw and
the historic Welsh Office functions now falling within the responsibility
of your Office.

I would be grateful for a substantive response addressing each of the
matters above individually.

Yours sincerely,


Sion Buckler (Ret’d Sergeant)

underlying question of title, evidence, procedure or institutional conduct

What happened to my family and our home in the 1980s was, in its human
consequences, devastating. From my perspective, it amounted to an assault
on our family itself. And decades of it. At least mid 40's by Western
Ground Rents and onwards.

For decades there has been no meaningful after-support, no meaningful
attempt at reconciliation, no reparative process and, above all, no
satisfactory account of what actually happened.

places remarkably difficult to obtain.

CADW is only one of numerous agencies about which my representatives are
now compiling material.

The emerging picture includes questions concerning procedural fairness,
court proceedings, evidential failures, institutional decision-making,
heritage protection and the apparent absence of effective oversight.

The more documents I obtain, the more questions arise.

And I am increasingly uncomfortable with the proposition that *the
descendants of the people affected should have to conduct the investigation
themselves simply to discover what the institutions already ought to know.*

It is particularly distressing that I am having to investigate matters
surrounding my own father's and grandmother's lives and deaths in this way.

I appreciate that officials have workloads.

I appreciate that nobody likes receiving an inconvenient historical file
with several decades' worth of questions attached to it.

It is not an answer.
