Dear Dr Wigley,

Thank you for your response and for the further clarification concerning
the surviving Cadw records and the historic retention arrangements.

Having considered your response alongside the evidence set out in my report
of 10 August, I think it is important to distinguish between two quite
separate propositions:

   1. *Cadw has released all records concerning the 1988 assessment which
   it can now locate*; and
   2. *the surviving records establish the evidential and administrative
   basis upon which the December 1988 decision was made.*

Your response appears to establish the first, but not the second.

That distinction is important because the surviving evidence is
exceptionally limited: two photographs. The absence of the underlying
assessment papers means that a number of historically significant questions
cannot now be answered from Cadw's records.

I am therefore asking for clarification of the position rather than asking
Cadw to recreate records which no longer exist.
1. What the surviving record establishes

Could Cadw please confirm whether the following is an accurate description
of the present evidential position:

*Cadw's surviving records do not establish the evidential or administrative
basis of the December 1988 decision not to list Great House Farm. In
particular, the surviving records do not establish what evidence was
considered by the inspector or decision-maker, whether the H.J. Thomas
RCAHMW survey of 26 April 1974 was considered, whether the relevant
SMR/GGAT archaeological material was considered, what inspection findings
were recorded in December 1988, or whether any internal recommendation or
consultation took place.*

If that is correct, I would be grateful if Cadw would confirm it expressly.

I am not suggesting that the absence of records proves that those matters
did not occur. Equally, however, the absence of records means that Cadw
cannot now establish that they did occur.

That is the central evidential limitation created by the loss of the 1988
working papers.
2. The 1974 H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey

Your response says:

"we are unable to determine whether or not the 1974 survey was taken into
account at the time."

That is a particularly important clarification.

The RCAHMW survey was not a document subsequently created in response to
the dispute. It was a professional survey undertaken on 26 April 1974 and
recorded architectural features including the late-17th-century
construction, Type A sub-medieval cross-passage plan, substantial timber
framing and the barrel-vaulted cellar.

I therefore ask Cadw to confirm simply:

*Cadw cannot now establish from its surviving records whether the inspector
or decision-maker responsible for the December 1988 assessment had
considered the H.J. Thomas survey before concluding that Great House Farm
was "not of sufficient architectural merit".*

If that is Cadw's position, I will record it as such.
3. The archaeological evidence

The same issue appears to arise in relation to the archaeological
assessment.

My report identifies evidence predating December 1988 concerning Roman,
Iron Age and medieval activity at the site, including the recorded SMR
material and the 1978–80 archaeological investigations.

I appreciate that the later 1994 excavation cannot simply be projected
backwards and treated as evidence which Cadw necessarily possessed in 1988.

The relevant question is narrower:

*Can Cadw now establish, from any surviving record, what archaeological
information was actually considered when the December 1988 conclusion was
reached that the site was "not of sufficient archaeological interest"?*

If it cannot, please confirm that this cannot now be established.

This would avoid conflating the later archaeological discoveries with the
separate question of what information was available to Cadw in 1988.
4. The July "YYY" coding

There remains an important unresolved point concerning the July 1988
photographs.

Cadw has previously explained that the "YYY" coding indicated that the
building did not meet the listing criteria. The photographs were taken on
29 July 1988.

The contemporary press report of 3 December 1988, however, records Cadw as
saying that it was then "considering" asking the Secretary of State to
protect Great House Farm as a listed building and that an inspector would
visit that weekend.

I appreciate that the records necessary to resolve this may no longer exist.

Nevertheless, could Cadw confirm whether it can establish:

   - what "YYY" specifically represented within the July 1988 process;
   - whether it was a final assessment or provisional coding;
   - whether it was applied by the July inspector;
   - whether the July assessment was subsequently reviewed in December; and
   - whether the December inspector had access to the July photographs or
   any associated assessment.

If none of these matters can now be established, I would be grateful for
that to be confirmed rather than inferred.
5. Identity of the December decision-maker

One further factual gap remains.

Can Cadw establish the identity of:

   - the inspector who undertook the December 1988 inspection; and
   - the person who made or authorised the decision communicated on 5
   December 1988 that Great House Farm was not of sufficient architectural
   merit and archaeological interest?

If the relevant individual(s) cannot now be identified from surviving
records, please confirm that.

This is not a request for personal information beyond what would ordinarily
form part of the historical administrative record. It is simply an attempt
to establish whether the decision itself can still be attributed to an
identifiable office-holder.
6. The retention explanation

I also wish to clarify an important qualification in your latest response.

You state that current colleagues have advised that, based on their
knowledge of the systems then in place, unsuccessful listing files were
*"likely"* to have been retained for approximately three years.

I understand that this is necessarily a reconstruction of historic practice
because the relevant records no longer exist.

Could you therefore confirm whether Cadw has located:

   - a 1980s retention schedule;
   - a disposal or destruction policy applicable to the relevant records;
   - a disposal schedule;
   - a destruction certificate or log;
   - a transfer/accession record to RCAHMW or another repository; or
   - any other contemporaneous record showing what happened to the Great
   House Farm material.

If none has been located, I would be grateful if Cadw could state expressly
that *the approximately three-year retention period is an account of the
general historic practice as presently understood by current staff, and not
documentary evidence establishing that the Great House Farm records were
actually destroyed after three years.*

That is an important distinction for the historical record.
7. What I am seeking from Cadw

I am not asking Cadw to speculate about matters for which the documentary
evidence has disappeared.

Indeed, the purpose of my report was deliberately to separate:



*what is established; what is a reasonable inference; and what can no
longer be verified because the records do not survive.*

Your latest response is helpful in establishing the third category.

I would therefore be grateful if Cadw could confirm, insofar as its records
permit, the following concise position:

*The surviving Cadw records relating to the December 1988 Great House Farm
assessment consist of two photographs. Cadw cannot now establish from
surviving records the detailed evidential or administrative basis of the
decision, including whether the 1974 H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey or relevant
archaeological records were considered. Cadw has not located records
establishing the disposal or transfer of the missing assessment material,
and the approximately three-year retention period represents the best
present understanding of historic practice rather than documentary evidence
concerning the disposal of this particular file.*

If that accurately reflects Cadw's position, I would regard that
clarification as extremely useful.
8. Historical record and next steps

I will separately approach Heneb concerning the Historic Environment
Record, as you have advised, and will pursue the question of any
appropriate heritage interpretation or marker with the relevant local
authority.

I also appreciate your clarification that Cadw cannot require or facilitate
installation of a marker.

My purpose in continuing this correspondence is therefore narrower than
seeking to reopen the FOI request. I am seeking to ensure that the
historical record does not inadvertently suggest that the absence of
surviving records means that the basis of the 1988 decision has been
established.

On the evidence presently available, the more accurate position appears to
be that *the decision is documented, but its underlying evidential and
administrative reasoning is no longer recoverable from Cadw's surviving
records.*

That is a significant historical finding in its own right.

Thank you again for your assistance. I would be grateful for confirmation
of the above points, particularly the status of the 1974 survey, the July
"YYY" coding, the identity of the December decision-maker, and the
evidential basis (if any) for the disposal of the missing records.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your latest correspondence dated 10th August in relation to your initial freedom of Information request (ATISN 27021) submitted in June 2026, which has been escalated to me for response.

As stated by my colleagues, I can confirm that all records we hold have been released to you. We do not hold any further records relating to the content or disposal of the historic records you have requested.

To confirm, colleagues in the records office have clarified the historic retention position to the best of their knowledge. Given that the issue relates to an historic record retention policy, and that no records regarding this are available, it is not possible to say exactly what CADW’s retention arrangements were over 38 years ago. However, based on their knowledge of the systems in place at the time, current colleagues have advised that it is likely that records of unsuccessful listings were only retained for a short period, usually about 3 years. This has since changed and current retention policy in relation to unsuccessful listings is to retain the files indefinitely, reviewed every 5 years.

In relation to your question ‘Did Cadw’s 1988 assessment of Great House Farm fully account for the independent professional evidence then available- particularly the H.J. Thomas RCAHMW survey of 1974- and if not why not?’. As stated, all of the records we hold have been released to you under the FOI and are now a public record. As the release consists of only two photographs we are unable to determine whether or not the 1974 survey was taken into account at the time.

In relation to question A, please see our previous emails of 2nd, 3rd, 10th and 29th July, together with the above explanation of the historic and current retention policies.

In relation to question B, content of the HER is managed by Heneb. Please contact www.heneb.org.uk<http://www.heneb.org.uk/> in relation to adding information to the HER.

In relation to question C, please refer to the FOI response provided on the 11th June 2026 which is a matter of public record and confirms Cadw’s position.

In relation to question D, noted above.

In relation to question E, Cadw are unable to require or facilitate the installation of a heritage marker at the site.

Yours sincerely,

Andy Wigley

Glamorgan Archives Team,

Further to my email of 22 August 2026 concerning the DBDT collection and
related Bute, Mountjoy and Western Ground Rents material (particularly
Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough), please treat this as an additional
request.




I have attached an image of the land parcel in question, believed to be in
the mislabelled record in question.

**Request: physical examination of DBDT79/1**

Catalogue entry:

Lease (counterpart) of land and premises situate in Pembroke Terrace,
Cardiff, from the Marquess of Bute to Mr John Williams, May 1877 [1
parchment, plan in margin].

Please examine the original document (not the catalogue description alone)
and confirm:

1. Parties and date – Does the original name the Marquess of Bute and Mr
John Williams, and is it dated May 1877?

2. Property description – Exact wording of the land and premises. Does it
expressly locate the property in Pembroke Terrace, Cardiff?

3. Llandough / other references – Any mention (body text, plan, schedule,
endorsements or annotations) of Llandough, Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr,
Western Ground Rents, or any locality outside Pembroke Terrace?

4. Marginal plan – Does the plan identify the location sufficiently? If
procedures allow, please supply a digital image or scan of the plan.

5. Further identifying details – Any adjoining owners, plot numbers,
parish, street numbers, measurements, previous ownership, rent,
consideration, or cross-references to other instruments.

If scanning is permitted, images of the parties clause, property
description and marginal plan would be ideal. Otherwise a transcription or
detailed description of those sections will suffice.


**Catalogue wording discrepancy**

Most other 1877 entries in the series describe the grantor as the “Trustees
of the Will of the late Marquess of Bute”. DBDT79/1 is catalogued simply as
“from the Marquess of Bute”.

From the original, please confirm:

- who executed the lease;

- the capacity in which the grantor is described;

- whether the Marquess is shown acting personally or through trustees;

- any evident reason for the difference from the other 1877 entries.

(I note the 3rd Marquess attained majority around this period, but I seek
the Archives’ evidence-based confirmation rather than assumption.)


**Purpose**

I am reconstructing the historical title position for Great House Farm / Tŷ
Mawr, Llandough, and need to distinguish any Cardiff property records from
those relating to the Llandough estate. Please report the physical contents
of DBDT79/1 separately from the catalogue description, noting any
differences.

Thank you for your assistance. I look forward to your response to both the
original enquiry and this request.


Also see attached a letter to my friend earlier today, which puts the
purpose of this enquiry and search and record and its importance into some
context for you. If you're at all interested. It might help you to unearth
records I'm unaware of.

There's 133 houses about to be developed on this land and their title maybe
defective. So please be diligent so that an egregious irreversible mistake
or injustice isn't made.

Regards,


Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
texts.gm-1a03ec02083c07d9:
Bev,

Thank you for the clarification. The distinction is important to my enquiry.

I am conducting a forensic reconstruction of the historical circumstances
surrounding the *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* dispute, including the events
surrounding Mary Doreen Williams, and her death in March 1983.

Mary died during the very short period in which she would have had an
opportunity to challenge the registration of her land in BP’s name. Her
ownership claim was never adjudicated or exstinguished. BP's award of
possession of her land (not ownership) resulted in a brutal dispossession
of her children and grandchildren resulting in a ECHR case in 1989, which
also prioritised BP's rights over the families.

I am therefore examining the documentary evidence concerning both the
land-registration dispute and the circumstances surrounding her death. I am
not suggesting from the timing alone that the two matters were connected;
rather, I am seeking to establish the underlying facts and ensure that the
surviving official record has been properly accounted for.

For that reason, I need to distinguish between *a historical absence of a
coronial record* and *the absence of a record from a modern computer system
which does not contain that historical material*.

I understand from your latest email that your computer system does not
store information concerning referrals received in 1983 or before. On that
basis, I understand that the search of your present system cannot establish
whether Mary Doreen Williams was or was not referred to the coroner.

Could I therefore clarify two points separately?

*1. Mary Doreen Williams — March 1983*

Does your office have any information concerning where the historical
records of the coroner responsible for Llandough Hospital in March 1983 are
now held, even if those records are no longer searchable by your office?

I am trying to establish the documentary chain:

*responsible coroner/jurisdiction → historical registers or case files →
transfer to archive or successor authority → present custodian, or
documented destruction/retention history.*

If you do not know the name of the coroner, could you identify the former
coroner’s jurisdiction or office responsible for Llandough Hospital at that
time? That would enable me to make a properly targeted request to the
relevant archive or records custodian.

You previously indicated that Glamorgan Archives may hold paper copies of
reports and post-mortem examination details. Could you clarify whether you
know that the historical Cardiff and Vale coronial records were actually
transferred to Glamorgan Archives, or whether Glamorgan Archives is being
suggested simply as the most likely repository?

If there is a known archive series, accession, register, transfer record or
other indication of where the former coroner’s records were deposited, that
information would be particularly helpful.

*2. William (Billy) Buckler — May 1990*

There is a separate point concerning William (Billy) Buckler, who died in
1990.

Your latest clarification refers specifically to information for referrals
received in *1983 or before*. As Billy died in 1990, could you please
clarify whether his case was capable of being searched in the computer
system you checked?

If it was searchable, I would be grateful if you could explain what the
negative result means — for example, whether no electronic record exists,
or whether the relevant Cardiff and Vale coronial records for that period
are held elsewhere.

Your earlier email stated:

“Cardiff and Vale cases prior to 2002 should be with the Glamorgan
Archivist.”

Could you please confirm whether that applies to Billy’s 1990 case as well?

More generally, I am trying to establish whether either death generated,
and whether there may now survive:

   - a referral to the coroner;
   - a coroner’s register entry or index;
   - a preliminary investigation or enquiry;
   - a post-mortem examination;
   - an inquest;
   - police, hospital or other official correspondence;
   - cause-of-death documentation;
   - coroner’s case papers; or
   - an archival transfer, retention or destruction record.

I appreciate that some underlying records may be subject to access
restrictions, and I am not asking your office to disclose confidential
medical information at this stage. My immediate objective is more
fundamental: *to establish whether a coronial record was created, whether
it survives, and what happened to it.*

That distinction is important to the historical investigation. A
present-day search producing no result is evidentially quite different from
a historical record establishing that no referral, investigation,
post-mortem or inquest ever took place.

I will now approach Glamorgan Archives, but any information you can provide
regarding the former coroner’s jurisdiction, the historical records held by
that jurisdiction, and their subsequent transfer or disposal would allow me
to make that request considerably more precise.

Thank you again for taking the time to clarify the position. Your latest
explanation has been genuinely helpful in establishing the limitations of
the present electronic search, and I appreciate your assistance in
identifying the surviving historical record.

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret’d Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your email requesting an internal review of our response to FOI 2026-024.

  *   an eastern cottages plot.

Dear Mr Buckler,

Thank you for your request for information received on 27 July 2026 concerning records relating to a reported discovery at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including a soldier, horse remains and items described as a visor and lance.

Amgueddfa Cymru has undertaken searches of its collections management systems, accession records and associated documentation.

We have not identified any records relating to the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or deposit of a medieval visor, lance, helmet or other item of armour associated with Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. We have also not identified records relating to the specific discovery described in your request, including records of associated human or animal remains, reburial records, excavation reports, watching briefs or discovery reports.

Accordingly, under section 1(1)(a) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, our response is that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold the requested information.

For completeness, our searches identified records relating to other archaeological finds from Church Farm, Llandough and to other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. These records do not relate to, nor are they otherwise associated with, the discovery described in your request. We have therefore not considered them to fall within the scope of this request.

If you are dissatisfied with this response, you may request an internal review by writing to [email redacted]<[email redacted]> within 40 working days of the date of this letter.

Dear Freedom of Information Team,

I am writing to request information under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and, where applicable, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004.

A published local history account states that, during works to replace the stone floor of the dining room at Great House Farm (also known as Ty Mawr), Llandough, Cardiff, the remains of a soldier and his horse were discovered beneath the floor.

 The remains were subsequently re-buried in the churchyard, and the soldier's visor and lance were given to the National Museum of Wales (Amgueddfa Cymru).

I therefore request the following recorded information held by Amgueddfa Cymru:

Any records relating to the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or deposit of a medieval visor, lance, helmet, or other items of armour associated with Great House Farm / Ty Mawr / Llandough.

The accession number(s), date of acquisition or transfer, name of the donor or transferring body, and any provenance or discovery notes linked to these objects.

Any catalogue entries, object records, or internal correspondence concerning the above items.

Any records of associated human or animal remains from the same discovery, including notes on reburial.

Any related excavation, watching-brief, or discovery reports held by the Museum.

If any of the requested information is already publicly available (for example via the Museum's online collections database), I would be grateful if you could simply provide the relevant accession numbers or catalogue links.

Please treat this as a request for recorded information only. I am not seeking advice or opinion.

I look forward to your response within the statutory timescale.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

> The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory
> basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of
> deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would
> not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024,
> when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales.
> From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal
> requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for
> deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service.
> Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor,
> with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that
> existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades
> later.
>
>
>
> If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records
> of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally
> public records.
>
>
>
> The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered
> with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In
> Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983
> if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained
> under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in
> 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical
> information.
>
>
>
> If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital,
> possible sources are:
>
>
>
>    1. Death certificate from the General Register Office.
>    2. Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
>    3. The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records,
>    now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
>    4. Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.
>
>
>
> In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the
> local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health
> Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area
> before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff &

Thursday 09.30 – 12.30 and 1.30 – 4.30

Ms Davidson,

Thank you for your further response. Very much appreciate your time in this
matter.

I have considered it carefully. I now need to make one fundamental point
clear. This is not any animosity or prejudice but a matter of upmost
importance to my family, many of whome are women and too frightened to
speak out. I must do my ahsolute best and part here and take the following
position on this matter.

I do not accept the characterisation of my complaint as being simply that a
councillor failed to answer a number of emails.

That formulation removes the very circumstances which made the conduct
complained of potentially relevant to the standards expected of an elected
member.

Councillor Carroll initially responded to me and asked how he could help. I
then provided the information and evidence requested. What followed was not
an isolated unanswered email, but a documented pattern of non-engagement
over approximately five months, notwithstanding repeated approaches
concerning matters affecting his own ward, including planning, development,
historical records and a serious concern that the title upon which current
development is proceeding may itself require examination.

I am not asking the Monitoring Officer to determine the ownership of Great
House Farm by correspondence. Nor am I asking the Council to accept my
allegations as established fact.

I am asking whether the conduct of an elected member, in the circumstances
actually presented, was properly assessed against the full range of
standards applicable to that member.
1. The Code cannot be reduced to an obligation to answer emails

I accept the proposition that the Members' Code does not create a general
rule requiring a councillor to answer every email received from a member of
the public within a prescribed period.

That is not the proposition I have advanced.

The question is whether a sustained course of conduct can engage provisions
of the Code concerning respect and consideration, conduct capable of
bringing the member's office or authority into disrepute, misuse of
position, and the broader principles governing the conduct of elected
representatives.

The Council's current Constitution places the Members' Code within Section
19 and separately identifies the principles governing members' conduct.

The Public Services Ombudsman for Wales itself describes the Code as
imposing enforceable minimum standards on councillors and identifies,
amongst other matters, conduct which negatively affects an authority's
reputation, unfair use of position, bullying, and failures to treat people
equally as matters which can potentially constitute breaches.

I therefore ask you to identify precisely which provisions you considered
and, more importantly, why the particular factual circumstances I supplied
were considered incapable of engaging any of them.

A conclusion that "failure to respond is not itself a breach" does not
answer that question.
2. The actual chronology matters

Please record the chronology accurately.

This was not:

five emails were sent and a councillor did not reply.

It was:

   - I approached my elected ward councillor concerning matters affecting
   his ward;
   - Councillor Carroll responded and asked how he could help;
   - I then supplied substantive information and evidence;
   - further correspondence followed on 16 February, 4 May, 7 June, 25 June
   and 13 July 2026;
   - the correspondence concerned, amongst other things, the historical
   planning and development of Great House Farm / Church View Close, access to
   relevant public records, and an apparent defect or inconsistency in the
   historical title chain;
   - despite the initial invitation to explain how he could assist, there
   was subsequently no substantive engagement with the matters raised.

That is the conduct I asked you to assess.

I therefore ask you to confirm whether you considered the actual underlying
emails and attachments, rather than merely the summary chronology.
3. Was Councillor Carroll's account obtained?

You have now confirmed that you did not consider it necessary to seek
comments from Councillor Carroll.

I appreciate that you do not have to conduct a full investigation at this
stage.

Nevertheless, that makes the precise nature of your decision particularly
important.

You have reached a conclusion that the information provided did not
disclose evidence capable of amounting to a breach, whilst apparently not
obtaining the explanation of the person whose conduct was complained of.

That does not necessarily make the decision unlawful. But it does mean that
I am entitled to understand precisely what factual inference you drew from
the material before you.

In particular, if there was a reason why Councillor Carroll did not respond
after initially offering to help, I do not know what that reason was.

If the reason was that he considered the matter outside his role, please
say so.

If the reason was that he considered the correspondence excessive,
vexatious or otherwise inappropriate, please say so.

If the reason was connected with material I had published or discussed on
social media, please say so.

If there was another reason, please identify it.

I am not alleging any particular explanation. I am asking that the factual
basis of the conduct not simply be assumed.
4. Social media and equal treatment

I also wish to place one specific issue on record.

I understand that the Code does not simply regulate everything a member or
member of the public says on social media. The Ombudsman itself has
separate guidance concerning social media and the Code.

Accordingly, if social-media material has influenced Councillor Carroll's
decision to disengage from me, I would ask that this be disclosed rather
than silently becoming the background justification for his conduct.

It would be an obvious inconsistency if material said or published by a
constituent outside the relevant Code framework were treated as a reason
for refusing to engage with that constituent, while the resulting conduct
of the elected member were then assessed in isolation as merely "a failure
to respond".

Again, I am not asserting that this occurred. I am asking that it not be
assumed away.
5. This is also a question of democratic accountability

There is a much wider issue here which I do not believe has been addressed.

I am raising a documented public-interest concern concerning land within
the Council's area, historical planning and enforcement records, the
demolition and subsequent development of Great House Farm / Church View
Close, and an apparent problem in the title history of land now associated
with substantial residential development.

I am not asking the Council to decide my private ownership claim.

I am asking that the concern be capable of being placed before the
democratic institutions of the Council and scrutinised by the appropriate
people.

The Council itself expressly operates mechanisms for public questions at
Full Council, and its published meeting material demonstrates that
questions from the public are part of its democratic process. The Council
also states that its meetings are conducted to support and promote
democratic engagement and public interest.

Your response says that no further action will be taken by you. It does
not, however, tell me what democratic route remains available for me to
place the underlying public-interest concern before elected members.

I therefore ask you to identify that route.

Specifically, please confirm how I may:

   1.

   submit a public question to Full Council concerning the Council's
   records and handling of this matter;
   2.

   submit a petition or e-petition;
   3.

   seek consideration by the appropriate Scrutiny Committee;
   4.

   raise the adequacy of the Council's handling of the matter with the
   Governance and Audit Committee or other appropriate constitutional body; and
   5.

   request inspection of relevant historical background papers associated
   with the planning and demolition history of the site.

The answer cannot simply be that the Monitoring Officer has decided not to
take further action. That determines one particular route. It does not
extinguish democratic accountability.
6. The public-record issue needs to be separated from the ownership dispute

I also want to avoid any further misunderstanding concerning the planning
records.

I have repeatedly encountered historical material which is not presently
accessible to me through the Council's online planning system.

I am not presently asserting that this proves deliberate concealment.

There may be perfectly legitimate explanations: age of the records,
digitisation, migration between systems, retention arrangements, technical
problems, or the fact that historical material was never placed online.

But the important point is that the Council's own planning-register
arrangements acknowledge that the online register is not necessarily a
complete database of everything held by the Council.

That makes the appropriate question one of transparency:

*What records does the Council hold, what records does it no longer hold,
where are the surviving records, and how can they be inspected?*

That is a straightforward public-record question.

It should not depend upon the Council first accepting my interpretation of
the title history.

I therefore intend to pursue the records question separately and formally,
including under the applicable information-access legislation where
appropriate.
7. The historical planning record is itself relevant

The historical demolition of Great House Farm is not an invented issue
arising solely from my family account.

The historic environment record identifies Great House Farm as a
historically significant site and records its sudden and complete
demolition in December 1988 amid considerable local controversy.

Whatever conclusion is ultimately reached concerning ownership, title or
the historical allegations, the existence of a significant historical
record means that it is reasonable to ask what planning, enforcement,
demolition, committee and officer records survive and what decisions were
made.

I am therefore not asking the Council to rewrite history in accordance with
my family's interpretation.

I am asking the Council to disclose its own documentary history.
8. Monitoring Officer responsibilities

I also ask you to clarify the extent to which you have considered the
Council's own potential obligations as an authority, as distinct from your
assessment of Councillor Carroll's individual conduct.

Section 5 of the Local Government and Housing Act 1989 places a statutory
reporting function upon a Monitoring Officer where it appears that a
proposal, decision or omission by the authority, its committees,
sub-committees, officers or other specified authority actors gives rise to
the statutory circumstances identified in that provision.

I am not asserting that section 5 automatically requires you to issue a
report merely because I have asked you to do so.

I am asking a narrower and more reasonable question:

*Have you considered whether any separate omission or decision by the
Council itself — particularly concerning access to public records,
democratic engagement or the handling of this matter — engages your
statutory Monitoring Officer responsibilities?*

If you have considered that question and concluded that section 5 is not
engaged, please say so and give the reason.

If you have not considered it, please confirm that.
9. The Ombudsman

Your response expressly directs me to the Public Services Ombudsman for
Wales.

I will therefore consider making a direct Code of Conduct complaint
supported by the underlying correspondence rather than relying upon the
Council's characterisation of the matter.

That is particularly appropriate because the Ombudsman states that its
initial assessment considers whether evidence suggests that a Code breach
may have occurred and, separately, whether investigation would be
sufficiently serious and in the public interest. The Ombudsman specifically
identifies maintaining public confidence in local councillors as one factor
relevant to that assessment.

I will therefore allow the Ombudsman to make its own assessment of the
evidence.

I will provide it with the actual chronology, the original correspondence,
the initial response from Councillor Carroll asking how he could assist,
the subsequent correspondence, and your decision.
10. One final point about the characterisation of my conduct

I have been persistent because I consider the underlying matter important.

Persistence should not be confused with misconduct.

The Ombudsman itself expressly states that it does not regard behaviour as
unacceptable merely because a complainant is forceful or determined, while
also making clear that correspondence should remain polite and courteous.

I accept the latter completely.

I am therefore going to continue to pursue these matters firmly, but
through the proper channels and on the evidence.

What I will not accept is the repeated administrative reframing of a
substantive public-interest concern as nothing more than an unhappy
constituent sending too many emails.
Accordingly, I ask you to confirm:

   1.

   The exact provisions of the Members' Code of Conduct which you
   considered.
   2.

   Whether you considered the five original emails and their attachments in
   full.
   3.

   Whether you considered Councillor Carroll's initial response asking how
   he could assist.
   4.

   Whether Councillor Carroll was asked for an explanation. If not, please
   confirm that.
   5.

   Whether you are aware of any reason why he subsequently ceased
   substantive engagement.
   6.

   Whether social-media activity formed any part of the reason for his
   non-engagement.
   7.

   Whether you have considered any potential omission or decision by the
   Council itself under your statutory Monitoring Officer responsibilities.
   8.

   What democratic mechanism you say is available for me to place the
   underlying public-interest concern before elected members.
   9.

   How I can obtain or inspect the surviving planning, enforcement,
   demolition, committee and officer records relating to Great House Farm /
   Church View Close which are not available through the online planning
   system.
   10.

   Whether any relevant records are known to have been destroyed, disposed
   of, transferred, archived elsewhere or otherwise become unavailable, and,
   if so, under what records-management arrangements.
   11.

   Whether the historical demolition and subsequent development were
   considered by a Council committee and, if so, where the relevant agendas,
   reports, minutes and background papers can be inspected.

I am deliberately keeping these questions precise because I want a proper
evidential record rather than another exchange in which the substance of
the issue is lost in administrative categorisation.

I am also not asking you to endorse my conclusions concerning title.

The democratic question is much simpler:

*Where a constituent places before his elected representative a documented
concern that land within the ward may be affected by a defective or
unresolved title history, and where the historical public records needed to
examine that concern are not readily accessible, what mechanism exists for
that concern to be transparently examined rather than simply closed
administratively?*

That question remains unanswered.

I would therefore be grateful for a substantive response to the points
above.

Yours sincerely,

*Sion Hywel Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*
*Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member*

Dear Mr Buckler



Thank you for your email. As the main contact for Freedom of Information, I have not seen your request previously but I will explain what I can in regards to your original request:



I am writing to enquire whether any records or references are held in relation to the following historical deaths that occurred in the Cardiff & Vale / Llandough area:

1. William (Billy) Buckler
   - Died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41
   - Reported cause: heart attack

2. Mary Doreen Williams
   - Born 10 August 1913
   - Death registered March 1983, South Glamorgan (Vol 28, Page 3029)

Although these pre-date the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if you could advise whether any legacy records, referrals, or related documentation exist, or direct me to the appropriate archive or department that may hold such information.



The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.



If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.



The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.



If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:



  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.



In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.



They can be contacted here:



Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board 



GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be out of scope.



I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are no records found for either patients due to the time elapsed.



Further comments have been provided below in red for reference.



I hope that this is an acceptable response.

> The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory
> basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of
> deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would
> not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024,
> when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales.
> From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal
> requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for
> deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service.
> Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor,
> with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that
> existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades
> later.
>
>
>
> If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records
> of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally
> public records.
>
>
>
> The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered
> with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In
> Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983
> if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained
> under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in
> 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical
> information.
>
>
>
> If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital,
> possible sources are:
>
>
>
>    1. Death certificate from the General Register Office.
>    2. Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
>    3. The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records,
>    now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
>    4. Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.
>
>
>
> In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the
> local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health
> Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area
> before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff &
> Vale University Health Board.
>
>
>
> They can be contacted here:
>
>
>
> Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board
>  
>
>
>
> GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS
> records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years
> after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be
> out of scope.

Dear Mr Buckler,
Thank you for your email.
I note your request for further clarification regarding my decision in my capacity as Monitoring Officer.
The assessment I undertook was limited to considering whether the information provided disclosed evidence which, if established, could indicate a failure by the member to comply with the statutory Member’s Code of Conduct. As Monitoring Officer, I do not have formal investigatory powers equivalent to those of the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales and I am not required to undertake an investigation or obtain representations from a member before deciding whether there is sufficient basis for a referral to be made. My role at this stage is to consider whether the information presented discloses evidence of conduct that appears capable of amounting to a breach of the Code.
In reaching my view, I considered the information provided within your complaint, including the chronology you supplied regarding correspondence sent to Councillor Carroll between February and July 2026. The substance of the complaint was that you had not received substantive responses to a number of emails sent over that period.
For completeness, I considered whether the conduct alleged could potentially engage any of the principal obligations contained within the Member's Code of Conduct. These include requirements that members show respect and consideration for others, do not engage in bullying, harassment or discriminatory behaviour, do not bring their office or authority into disrepute, do not improperly use their position to confer an advantage or disadvantage on any person, and do not misuse Council resources or confidential information.
Whilst I appreciate that the absence of a response to correspondence may be frustrating, the information provided did not disclose evidence of disrespectful behaviour, bullying, harassment, misuse of position, misuse of Council resources, disclosure of confidential information, conduct bringing the office of member or the authority into disrepute, or any other behaviour which appeared capable of amounting to a breach of the Code. In reaching that view, I considered the nature of the conduct alleged, namely a failure to respond to correspondence, and whether that conduct engaged any provision of the Code.
It is important to note that the Member’s Code of Conduct does not impose a general obligation on elected members to respond to all correspondence received from members of the public, nor does it prescribe timescales within which responses must be provided. The Code is concerned with standards of conduct rather than the quality, adequacy or timeliness of constituency casework. Consequently, a decision not to respond, or not to respond in the manner sought by a correspondent, does not of itself constitute evidence of a breach of the Code.
Given that the information provided did not disclose evidence which appeared capable of amounting to a breach of the Code, I did not consider it necessary or proportionate to seek comments from Councillor Carroll before reaching that conclusion. My decision was therefore based upon the information contained within your complaint and whether that information, taken at its highest, indicated a potential breach of the Code warranting further action.
For completeness, any person is entitled to submit a complaint directly to the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales if they believe a member has failed to comply with the Member’s Code of Conduct. The Ombudsman is independent of the Council and is responsible for determining whether a complaint should be investigated and, if so, whether any further action is appropriate.
I trust this clarifies the basis of my decision. Having reviewed the information provided, my position remains that I have not identified evidence which would justify further action by me in my capacity as Monitoring Officer.
Yours sincerely,

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your email. As the main contact for Freedom of Information, I have not seen your request previously but I will explain what I can in regards to your original request:

I am writing to enquire whether any records or references are held in relation to the following historical deaths that occurred in the Cardiff & Vale / Llandough area:

1. William (Billy) Buckler
   - Died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41
   - Reported cause: heart attack

2. Mary Doreen Williams
   - Born 10 August 1913
   - Death registered March 1983, South Glamorgan (Vol 28, Page 3029)

Although these pre-date the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if you could advise whether any legacy records, referrals, or related documentation exist, or direct me to the appropriate archive or department that may hold such information.

The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.

If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.

The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.

If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:


  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.

In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.

They can be contacted here:

Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board 

GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be out of scope.

I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are no records found for either patients due to the time elapsed.

Further comments have been provided below in red for reference.

I hope that this is an acceptable response.
